It starts with a whole project in one picture, then explains tokens, transformers, how a model sees images and hears speech, and what omni models are. Next come LoRA and QLoRA on a free sixteen gigabyte T4, and then data, metrics, normalization and fairness for your experiments. It closes with a map of all eleven papers and a glossary. After this tab come QLoRA, the fine-tuning tool, then the vision language models TinyLLaVA Factory and SmolVLM, the speech models Voxtral and Voxtral Realtime, the efficient backbone LFM2, and the omni models MiniMind-O, Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3-Omni, MiniCPM-o 4.5 and Gemma 4. text: A model never sees letters, only vectors. The tokenizer cuts the sentence into sub-word pieces, often with the leading space attached, and each piece has a fixed ID in the vocabulary. The embedding table then turns each ID into a vector of d numbers, where d is the model's width. The IDs shown are illustrative. The practical lesson is simple: always use the tokenizer and processor that ship with your checkpoint.

label: Primer
text: Everything a language model does comes from predicting the next token. On the left, the model gives a probability to every possible next token, picks one, appends it and repeats. On the right is the chat template, where system, user and assistant turns are marked with special tokens, and image and audio tokens sit inside the user turn. Instruction-tuned models were trained in this format, so your fine-tuning data must use it too, with the loss on the answer only.

section: Transformers and language models in 5 minutes
text: Attention is how tokens share information. The word it sends a query, compares it with the key of every other word, and pulls in most from cat, shown by the thickest line. Every token does this at the same time in every layer. The weights here are illustrative. This matters for you because image and audio tokens take part in the same attention, which is how the model connects your spoken question to the picture.

label: Primer
section: Transformers and language models in 5 minutes
text: A decoder language model is a stack of identical layers. Tokens are embedded, pass through L layers that each contain an attention block and a feed-forward block, and an output head turns the result into next-token probabilities. The parameters are the numbers in the weight matrices of these linear layers, so a two billion parameter model holds about two billion of them. Those same linear layers are where LoRA adapters attach in section seven.

section: Transformers and language models in 5 minutes
text: Images and audio fill the context much faster than text. A typed question is only about fifteen tokens, but thirty seconds of speech costs three hundred to about seven hundred and fifty tokens and one tiled image in LFM2-VL costs about two thousand eight hundred. Pixel shuffle brings a SmolVLM tile from one thousand and twenty four tokens down to sixty four. Because training memory grows with sequence length, these bars predict whether your run fits on a T4.

section: Transformers and language models in 5 minutes
text: This is the attention formula. Q holds the queries, K the keys and V the values. Multiplying Q by K transposed scores every pair of tokens, dividing by the square root of d k keeps the scores in a stable range, and softmax turns each row into weights that sum to one. The output mixes the values with those weights. The score matrix is tokens by tokens, so cost grows with the square of the sequence length.

section: Transformers and language models in 5 minutes
text: Weight memory is roughly the number of parameters times the bytes used for each one. A two billion parameter model at two bytes per parameter, which is FP16, needs about four gigabytes, and in four bits, half a byte each, about one gigabyte plus a little for scale constants. This one line explains why QLoRA stores the frozen model in four bits, and it is the first check before you pick a model for the free T4.

section: Transformers and language models in 5 minutes
text: The table applies the memory rule to a two billion and a seven billion parameter model at four precisions. Read across a row: each halving of the bytes halves the memory, from twenty eight gigabytes for a seven billion model in FP32 down to about three and a half in four-bit NF4. These are weights only. Training adds gradients, optimizer states and activations, and remember that the T4 runs FP16 but not fast BF16.

text: Here is the path from pixels to tokens. The image is cut into sixteen by sixteen pixel patches, so a five hundred and twelve pixel square gives one thousand and twenty four patches. A frozen vision transformer such as SigLIP turns them into features, a compression step cuts their number, and a small trainable projector maps them into the language model's embedding space. The resulting visual tokens sit beside the text tokens,, and the language model reads both.

label: Primer
text: Two knobs set how many tokens an image costs. Tiling splits a large image into tiles plus a small thumbnail so fine text stays readable, at five times the tokens. Pixel shuffle folds each r by r block of features into one wider token, dividing the count by r squared: four for r equal two, sixteen for SmolVLM's r equal four. On a sixteen gigabyte GPU, fewer tiles is an easy saving, but document and OCR tasks suffer first.

section: How a model hears and speaks
text: Audio enters the model the same way images do. The sixteen kilohertz waveform becomes a log-mel spectrogram, a picture of energy per frequency band over time at one hundred frames per second. A Whisper-style encoder turns it into fifty frames per second, and a small adapter stacks four frames into one, giving twelve and a half audio tokens per second in Voxtral. So thirty seconds of speech becomes three hundred and seventy five tokens next to your text.

section: How a model hears and speaks
text: The cascade on the top left transcribes first, so tone is lost and speech recognition mistakes pass straight on; the native route on the top right lets the language model hear the audio tokens itself. Bottom left, a Talker produces codec tokens that a decoder turns into sound. Bottom right, a streaming model writes text a fixed delay tau behind the speaker, while an offline model waits for the end. Most fine-tuning tasks are offline.

label: Primer
text: An omni model puts every encoder in front of one language model called the Thinker. Text, images, video frames and audio pass through frozen encoders and small projectors, and the Thinker reasons over all of them and writes the text answer. A separate Talker reads the Thinker's hidden states and produces speech. Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3-Omni and MiniMind-O follow this design. For most fine-tuning tasks you need only text, so the Talker can stay frozen or unloaded.

label: Primer
text: This flow helps you choose a route. First ask whether your model accepts voice. If it does, use its native audio input; if not, put a speech-to-text model in front of a vision language model. Then ask whether it fits sixteen gigabytes with QLoRA; if not, use the smallest variant, shorter inputs, or rent a bigger GPU. The bottom line states the trade-off: pipelines are simple but pass on transcription errors, native models hear the audio but are bigger.

text: Three ways to fine-tune one weight matrix. Full fine-tuning trains every number in W, so each needs a gradient and optimizer states. LoRA freezes W and trains two thin matrices, B and A, whose product is added to it; at width two thousand and forty eight and rank sixteen, that is sixty five thousand numbers instead of four million. QLoRA keeps the same adapters but stores the frozen W in four-bit NF4, cutting weight memory to about a quarter.

This is the LoRA update. The new weight W prime equals the frozen weight W plus B times A, scaled by alpha over r. B has d rows and r columns, A has r rows and k columns, and the rank r is much smaller than both sides, so only r times d plus k numbers are trained. QLoRA's recipe uses rank sixty four and alpha sixteen, and found that adapters on every linear layer matter more than the rank.

label: Primer
text: In a multimodal model you freeze the senses and adapt the brain. The vision and audio encoders stay frozen, the small projectors or adapters can be trained fully, and LoRA goes on the language model's attention and feed-forward projections. The Talker, if there is one, stays frozen. One trap: setting target modules to all linear layers also hits the encoders, so list the language model's module names. These are the tabs' recommendations, so report whatever choice you make.

text: Good experiments start with a clean split. A few hundred training examples and a held-out test set, each combining an image, audio, a question and an answer, with the source and licence stated. Keep the same photo or speaker out of both sides, and record group labels now for the fairness test. On the right, the base model and the fine-tuned model are scored on the identical test set, with the same prompt, metric and normalization; the difference is your result.

Word error rate counts the edits needed to turn the model's transcript into the reference. S is substitutions, D is deletions and I is insertions, and their sum is divided by N, the number of words in the reference. Lower is better, and because insertions have no limit it can go above one hundred percent. Character error rate is the same idea on characters. The next figure works through one example by hand.

F one combines precision and recall into one number. Precision P is the share of your predicted items that are correct, true positives over true plus false positives. Recall R is the share of correct items you found, true positives over true positives plus false negatives. F one is two P R over P plus R, their harmonic mean. For short text answers it is often computed on overlapping words, while exact match only credits identical answers.

label: Primer
text: Here is word error rate done by hand. The reference has six words. The model writes sit instead of sat, a substitution, drops the second the, a deletion, and adds today, an insertion. Three edits over six words gives fifty percent. Libraries such as jiwer find this alignment automatically, but showing one example like this in your report proves you understand the metric you are using.

label: Primer
text: Normalization can change a score more than training does. The reference says It's 25 dollars with a full stop, and the model says its twenty five dollars. Raw, that is four edits over three words, one hundred and thirty three percent. After lowercasing, removing punctuation and writing numbers one way, the two strings are identical and the error is zero. A useful experiment is to train with and without normalized labels, then score both runs with one fixed scorer.

QLoRA asks whether you can finetune a large language model on a single GPU without losing the quality of full sixteen bit finetuning. Its answer is yes: freeze the model, store its weights in a new four bit data type called NormalFloat, and train only small low-rank adapters on every linear layer. The tab starts with the big picture, then the memory problem, the method in four steps, every equation, the six figures redrawn, the result tables, and finally a box that turns the paper into practical advice. QLoRA opens the atlas of eleven papers because it is the fine-tuning tool the other papers build on in practice. After it come the vision language models TinyLLaVA Factory and SmolVLM, the speech models Voxtral and Voxtral Realtime, LFM2, and the omni models MiniMind-O, Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3-Omni, MiniCPM-o 4.5 and Gemma 4.

label: Overview
text: The whole method in one picture: the model's brain stays frozen in four bits, and small rust coloured LoRA adapters beside every weight matrix do the learning. Only text goes in and only text comes out, so image, voice and video are greyed out as not supported. The zoom at the bottom is equation five: the frozen path dequantizes W to sixteen bits for the multiply, and the adapter path adds its small correction.

label: Problem A
text: Full sixteen bit finetuning of a sixty five billion parameter model needs more than 780 gigabytes of GPU memory, because every weight carries gradients and Adam states. QLoRA brings the same job under 48 gigabytes, one professional GPU. The dashed marker for the free Colab T4 at sixteen gigabytes shows why you will work with much smaller models.

label: Problem B
text: Absmax quantization, from equation one, stretches the grid to reach the largest value, so a single outlier leaves most of the sixteen four bit levels empty. The lower row shows the standard fix: cut the tensor into blocks and give each block its own scale. QLoRA uses blocks of sixty four weights, which creates many constants, the problem that double quantization later solves.

label: Problem C
text: For a seven billion parameter LLaMA the LoRA weights take only 26 megabytes, while the four bit base model takes about five thousand. Gradient checkpointing shrinks the input gradients from 567 megabytes to about 18 per sequence. The lesson the authors draw is that shrinking the frozen base is what saves memory, and adding more adapters costs almost nothing.

The procedure has a one-time part and a training part. Once, you build the NF4 grid, quantize every frozen weight in blocks of sixty four, and compress the block constants again with double quantization. Then you attach LoRA to every linear layer and train: weights are dequantized to sixteen bits on the fly, only adapters get gradients, and optimizer states page to CPU memory if a long batch would overflow the GPU.

label: Method 1
text: NF4 places its sixteen levels where trained weights actually are, crowded near zero and sparse in the tails. The magenta ticks are the exact values from Appendix E; each shaded band holds about the same share of normally distributed weights, so no level is wasted. The evenly spaced grey grid below is what plain integer four bit would use. This is the data type behind equation four.

label: Method 2
text: Double quantization squeezes the scales themselves. Each block of sixty four weights has a thirty two bit constant, which costs half a bit per weight. QLoRA groups 256 of these constants, centres them, and stores them in eight bit floats with one thirty two bit constant per group, cutting the overhead to 0.127 bits, about three gigabytes saved on a sixty five billion model.

label: Method 3
text: A long training sequence can briefly push GPU memory above its limit, which normally crashes the run. With paged optimizers the Adam states live in NVIDIA unified memory, so pages are evicted to CPU RAM during the spike and brought back for the optimizer step. The drawing is schematic; the paper reports no slowdown for a sixty five billion model at batch size sixteen.

label: Method 4
text: QLoRA stores weights in four bit NF4 but computes in sixteen bit brain float. Every use of a weight dequantizes it first. In the backward pass the gradient still travels through W to earlier layers, but no gradient for W itself is computed. Only the adapter matrices L one and L two receive gradients and optimizer updates, which is why memory stays small.

This block turns the paper's Appendix B settings into the Hugging Face configuration you will actually type. The quantization config asks for NF4 with double quantization, the LoRA config puts rank sixty four adapters with alpha sixteen on all linear layers, and the training arguments pick the paged AdamW optimizer, a constant learning rate of two times ten to the minus four, and gradient clipping at 0.3. On a T4, switch the compute type to float sixteen.

Equation one is ordinary absmax quantization to eight bit integers. X FP32 is the full precision tensor; it is multiplied by 127 divided by its largest absolute value, and rounded. That factor is the quantization constant c. Because the largest value sets the scale, outliers waste the grid, which motivates blockwise quantization and, later, NF4.

Equation two undoes equation one: divide the stored integers by the same constant c to get back the full precision values, up to rounding error. QLoRA performs this dequantization every time a frozen weight is used, and equation six applies it twice.

The input tensor X, with b rows and h columns, is flattened and cut into n blocks of size B, so n equals b times h divided by B. Each block gets its own constant c i. Smaller blocks limit the damage of an outlier but create more constants to store.

Equation three is LoRA. Y equals X times the frozen weight W, plus s times X times L one times L two. L one has h rows and r columns, L two has r rows and o columns, and r, the rank, is small, so the correction has few parameters. The scalar s scales the update. Only L one and L two are trained.

Equation four builds the NF4 levels. Q X is the quantile function of the standard normal distribution. Each level q i is the average of two neighbouring quantiles, so every bin catches the same expected number of normally distributed weights. With k equal to four this gives sixteen levels before normalizing them to the range minus one to one.

A symmetric grid from equation four has no exact zero, yet zero matters for padding and zero weights. So QLoRA takes eight levels for the negative side and nine for the positive side, merges them, and drops the duplicated zero. The result is exactly sixteen values, the NF4 table in Appendix E.

This line counts the cost of the quantization constants. Thirty two bits for every sixty four weights is half a bit per parameter. After double quantization it is eight over sixty four plus thirty two over sixty four times 256, which is 0.127 bits, a saving of 0.373 bits per parameter.

Equation five is QLoRA for one linear layer. The sixteen bit input X is multiplied by the double dequantized frozen weight, recovered from the NF4 weights and the two levels of constants c one and c two, and the adapter path X times L one times L two is added. It is exactly the zoom panel in the big picture.

Equation six defines double dequantization. First the eight bit block constants c two are recovered using the thirty two bit constant c one. Then those constants dequantize the four bit weights into a sixteen bit weight matrix. Weights use NF4 with blocks of sixty four, constants use FP8 with blocks of 256.

Training needs the gradient of the error E with respect to the adapter matrices L i, but not with respect to the frozen weights W. Computing the adapter gradient still requires passing gradients back through W, done in sixteen bit after dequantizing. This is why no optimizer state is needed for the base model.

This is the standard Elo formula behind the chatbot tournaments in Tables one and seven. E A is the expected win chance of model A given ratings R A and R B; after each match the rating moves by K times the surprise. The paper uses K of thirty two and a start of one thousand but does not print the formula itself.

Each cell of Table twelve compares two systems: the number of times GPT-4 judged row x better than column y, minus the times it judged y better, divided by the total number of judgments. A value near one means x almost always wins, near zero means a tie.

The frozen four bit model is seventy three to eighty one percent; the Adam states for the adapters come next. The seven billion model needs about 6.9 gigabytes in total, a useful anchor for what fits on a free GPU.

label: Chart A
text: Among four bit data types, NF4 with double quantization gives the lowest mean perplexity, 27.41, against 34.34 for integer four bit and around thirty for the two float four bit variants. Lower is better. It summarises Table two and supports the claim that NF4 is the most precise four bit grid for normally distributed weights.

label: Chart B
text: Three dot colours per column compare sixteen bit LoRA, float four bit QLoRA and NF4 QLoRA on MMLU for LLaMA seven to sixty five billion, trained on Alpaca or FLAN v2. The magenta NF4 dots sit on or above the black sixteen bit dots, while grey float four bit often falls below. On average NF4 scores 53.1, sixteen bit 53.0, float four bit 52.2.

label: Chart C
text: Guanaco, the chatbot family trained with QLoRA on the small OASST1 dataset, reaches 99.3 percent of ChatGPT's score at sixty five billion parameters in 41 gigabytes, and 87 percent at seven billion in just five. Bars are GPT-4 judged scores relative to ChatGPT. The confidence intervals of four to five points overlap, so treat close bars as ties.

Table one ranks chatbots by Elo rating from GPT-4 judged matches on the Vicuna prompts. GPT-4 is far ahead at 1348; Guanaco sixty five and thirty three billion come next, above Vicuna and ChatGPT. The size column shows the four bit Guanaco models need far less memory than sixteen bit Vicuna. Note that Table seven gives slightly different numbers for some models.

Table two compares four bit data types by the mean perplexity of quantized OPT, BLOOM, LLaMA and Pythia models from 125 million to 13 billion parameters. NF4 with double quantization wins with 27.41. It is the numeric backbone of the claim that NF4 is better than integer or float four bit.

Table three is the key fidelity test. On GLUE with RoBERTa and on Super-NaturalInstructions with T5 models up to eleven billion, sixteen bit full finetuning, sixteen bit LoRA and four bit QLoRA all land within about a point of each other. The performance lost by quantizing is recovered by training adapters on top.

Table four repeats the fidelity test at scale on MMLU, for LLaMA seven to sixty five billion trained on Alpaca and FLAN v2. NF4 with double quantization averages 53.1, matching sixteen bit LoRA at 53.0, while float four bit trails at 52.2. This is the strongest evidence that four bit QLoRA costs nothing in accuracy.

Table five shows MMLU after QLoRA finetuning on each of the eight instruction datasets. FLAN v2 is best on MMLU at every size, yet Table six shows it is among the worst chatbots. The lesson for you is that the right dataset depends on the task and the metric, not on popularity or size.

Table six scores every system on the Vicuna prompts as a percentage of ChatGPT, judged by GPT-4 in both presentation orders. Guanaco models trained on OASST1 top every size group, while the same base models trained on FLAN v2 score below fifty percent. The memory column shows the four bit models are several times smaller than sixteen bit baselines.

Table seven runs the Elo tournament with human raters and GPT-4 on two benchmarks. The Guanaco models rank just below GPT-4, often above ChatGPT. Humans and GPT-4 disagree on some models, especially Guanaco seven billion, and GPT-4 rates itself much higher than humans do, a bias worth remembering if you use a language model as a judge.

Table eight is the paper's only fairness check: the CrowS benchmark measures how likely a model is to produce stereotyped sentences in nine categories, lower is better. Guanaco sixty five billion averages 43.5 against 66.6 for its LLaMA base, so finetuning changed bias a lot. The paper warns that other kinds of bias were not tested.

Table nine lists the training hyperparameters per model size and dataset: batch size, learning rate, number of steps and maximum source and target lengths. Seven and thirteen billion models used a learning rate of two times ten to the minus four and batch sixteen; larger models halve the rate. Use the seven billion rows as a starting point for small models.

Table ten tests whether to compute the loss on the instruction as well as the answer. Training on the answer only wins on all four datasets, raising mean MMLU from 37.5 to 38.6. For your own fine-tuning, this means masking the prompt tokens so the model learns to produce answers.

Table eleven varies dataset size from fifty to 150 thousand examples and training from one to three epochs. Changing size or epochs moves MMLU by at most half a point, while switching datasets moves it by up to eight points. Quality and suitability of data beat quantity, reassuring news when you only have a few hundred examples.

Table twelve aggregates GPT-4's pairwise judgments between seven systems, using the formula from the equations section. Positive cells mean the row system usually wins. Guanaco sixty five billion beats every other system, and the judgments are transitive, which lets the authors derive the clean ordering in Table thirteen.

Table thirteen is the complete ranking implied by the pairwise GPT-4 judgments: Guanaco sixty five and thirty three billion first, then Vicuna, ChatGPT, Bard, and the smaller Guanacos. Model sizes are listed to show that the four bit thirty three billion Guanaco at 21 gigabytes outranks the sixteen bit Vicuna at 26.

text: Memory on a GPU is decided by how many bits store each weight. The bars show the weights of a seven billion parameter model: twenty eight gigabytes in thirty two bit floats, fourteen in sixteen bit, and three and a half in four bit. The dashed line is the sixteen gigabytes of a free Colab T4. Training also needs gradients and optimizer states, so on a free GPU you must shrink the frozen weights and train only a few.

label: Primer
text: Quantization is rounding. Four bits can name only sixteen values, so each real weight, a blue dot, is scaled and snapped to the nearest allowed level, a magenta tick. These ticks are the NF4 levels, crowded near zero where most weights sit. The model stores only the four bit code and one scale per block, and turns the weight back into sixteen bit numbers each time the layer runs, which is why accuracy survives.

label: Primer
text: LoRA leaves the big weight matrix W frozen and learns two thin matrices, L one and L two, whose product is added to the layer's output. With a four thousand by four thousand matrix and rank sixteen, you train about 131 thousand numbers instead of 16.8 million, less than one percent. Only the rust parts receive gradients and optimizer states. In a typical project these adapters are the only thing your notebook actually trains.

text: QLoRA is the first of eleven papers in the atlas, and it is a tool rather than a model. It handles text only: the paper fine-tunes language models that read and write text. The next tab, TinyLLaVA Factory, shows how an image encoder joins a small language model, and later tabs add voice. In practice you apply the QLoRA recipe to one of those multimodal models, or to a pipeline.

These fourteen terms are the vocabulary the paper takes for granted. The core ones are LoRA and its rank, quantization and the NF4 data type, double quantization and paged optimizers. BF16 is the sixteen bit format used for computing, though on a Colab T4 you will use FP16. MMLU, the Vicuna benchmark, Elo ratings and Guanaco appear in the results. Come back here whenever a term in the tab stops you.

TinyLLaVA Factory asks a practical question: how can a small team build, train and compare small vision-language models without rewriting code for every change? Its answer is a modular codebase in which the vision tower, the connector, the small language model, the chat template and the training recipe are each a swappable factory picked in a config file. It is software rather than a new model, and it reproduces the TinyLLaVA models slightly better than the original code. The tab moves from the big picture and the problem, through the method, a few background equations, the one figure, and the results, to a box of practical advice. Among the eleven papers it comes second, right after QLoRA, and opens the group on seeing, followed by SmolVLM. Teal is the image path: resize, a vision tower such as SigLIP, then a small MLP connector that turns image features into visual tokens. Indigo is the text path: the chat template and the model's own embeddings. Both streams meet in one small language model, which only writes text. The grey boxes are the gap you must fill: no voice, no video, no speech output, so a speech-to-text model feeds its transcript into the text path.

The problem is software design, not accuracy. On the left, the original LLaVA code makes the vision tower and connector properties of the language model, so changing one part means editing model code. On the right, the three parts are peers, each built by its own factory, with room for new parts later. Everything in the method section is a consequence of this one refactor.

Here is the factory pattern itself, which the codebase repeats everywhere. A config file names a module, the magenta factory looks that name up in a registry, and it builds a subclass of a shared base class. Phi, Llama and Gemma differ only where they must. The dashed rust box is your own module: inherit the base, register it, name it in the config. The list on the right shows the same trick for templates, towers, connectors and recipes.

This is how text enters the model and what it is trained on. A LLaVA-format sample becomes a prompt with a system message, is tokenized by the language model's tokenizer, and gets labels. The strip below shows the result: system, image and question tokens are masked, and only the answer tokens carry the loss. That is why each model family needs its own template, and it is exactly what background equation B2 writes down.

Read this grid as a switchboard: grey means frozen, rust means trained. In both of the paper's recipes the vision tower never trains. The last row is not from the paper; it shows how the built-in LoRA and QLoRA recipes would put small adapters on a frozen model, which is your setup.

These six steps are the life of one training run in the codebase. label: (B2)
text: Also background, not from the paper. The loss is the usual next-token loss: the negative sum of log probabilities of each token given the visual tokens and all earlier tokens. Keep this glossary open while you read. The key terms are vision tower, the image encoder; connector, the small network that turns image features into tokens; and chat template, the text format that decides which tokens are the training target. The benchmark names, such as TextVQA, POPE and MME, appear in the results table, and knowing what each one tests will help you choose your own metric.

SmolVLM asks how small a vision-language model can be while still reading documents, charts and videos well, and why small models built by shrinking big ones waste so much memory. Its answer is to redesign every choice for small scale: a small image encoder, a longer context, very aggressive compression of image tokens, image splitting, learned tile-position tokens and a carefully balanced data mix. The smallest model, with 256 million parameters, runs in under one gigabyte of GPU memory. The tab moves from the big picture and the problem, through the method, the few key relations, every figure and the results tables, to a box on using SmolVLM in practice. Among the eleven papers it is the third, after QLoRA and TinyLLaVA Factory, and the last pure vision model before the speech papers, starting with Voxtral. Keep in mind that it accepts text, images and video, but no voice.

Read this diagram row by row: each row is one kind of input travelling left to right into the same language model. Text goes straight through the tokenizer. Images and video frames go through the teal SigLIP encoder, the magenta pixel shuffle and a small projector. The top gold row is empty inside SmolVLM: there is no audio encoder and no speech output, so for a voice task the dashed speech-to-text add-on turns voice into text first.

The bars count tokens for one high-resolution image. One 512 by 512 tile already costs 1,024 tokens, half of the original two thousand token window of SmolLM2, and a split document with several tiles overflows it five times over. Pixel shuffle with a ratio of four brings the same image down to about 320 tokens. The tile count here is illustrative. This is the core problem the whole method attacks.

Indigo is the language model, teal the vision encoder, drawn to scale in parameters. With the tiniest 135 million parameter language model, the big 428 million encoder is three times larger than the model that has to reason, and scores drop. At 360 million it buys 11.6 percent more performance for 66 percent more parameters, and only at 1.7 billion does it become cheap. This motivates Finding 1.

These eight steps are the whole SmolVLM recipe in order of the paper. The first four are architecture: balance encoder and language model, stretch the context, compress image tokens, and split images but not videos. The next two are about how the input is written: learned tile tokens and a structured prompt with loss only on answers. The last two are about data and training stages. Each step is backed by one of the nine findings in the table below.

One training example laid out as a token sequence. Indigo blocks are plain text, magenta blocks are the learned tile-position tokens, teal blocks are visual tokens, and rust blocks are the answer. Only the rust part carries loss, because the user prompt is masked. When you fine-tune, keep exactly this format, which the model's processor produces for you, and train only on the answer tokens.

Training runs in two stages. The vision stage is mostly image data, with almost half of it about OCR and documents, plus fourteen percent text. The video stage mixes video, images, multi-image examples and text. The figure's twenty percent text disagrees with the fourteen percent stated in the paper's text, which the tab flags. The paper does not say which modules are frozen in each stage.

This pseudo-code is reconstructed from sections two and three, because the paper has no algorithm box. Follow the flow: every image becomes tiles plus a global view, every video becomes sampled frames, each tile goes through the encoder, pixel shuffle and projector, and the resulting visual tokens are placed in the sequence after a tile-position token, wrapped by intro and outro text. The language model then generates text only.

The paper is organised as nine findings, each a short rule for small multimodal models, and this table maps each one to the figure that supports it. Findings one to four are about architecture, five and six about how inputs and prompts are tokenized, and seven to nine about training data. Use it as a checklist when you design your own fine-tuning setup.

label: (A)
text: N patch equals H over p times W over p: the number of image tokens a vision transformer produces is the image height divided by the patch size, times the width divided by the patch size. For a 512 pixel image and SigLIP's patch size of 16, that is 32 times 32, or 1,024 tokens. This number is why image tokens flood a small context.

label: (B)
text: Pixel shuffle rearranges a feature map of height h, width w and d channels into one of height h over r, width w over r and d times r squared channels. Nothing is thrown away, but the number of positions, which are the visual tokens, falls by a factor of r squared. With r equal to four that is a sixteen-fold cut. This is the paper's main compression tool.

label: (C)
text: Putting the two relations together: 1,024 patch tokens divided by four squared gives 64 visual tokens for each 512 pixel tile at a shuffle ratio of four. The paper does not print this number, so treat it as a derived estimate for the small variants. It explains why the language model can afford many tiles or frames.

label: (D)
text: Rotary position embeddings rotate each pair of dimensions at a frequency theta i, equal to the base b raised to minus two i over the head dimension. The paper raises the base b from ten thousand to 273 thousand, which slows the rotations so the model can tell apart positions over a much longer sequence. This is how SmolLM2's context grew from two thousand to eight or sixteen thousand tokens.

label: (E)
text: The fine-tuning loss is the usual next-token loss, minus the log probability of each token y t given the tokens before it, but multiplied by a mask m t. The mask is one for tokens in the assistant's answer and zero everywhere else. So the model is never trained to reproduce the question or the image tokens. The paper states this in words as Finding 6, and it is the setting you should use.

That setup is a practical choice, not a rule from the paper.

label: Primer

SmolVLM keeps that recipe but redesigns every choice for tiny models, spends far fewer tokens per image, and adds video. The chips on the right show the gap: text and image, but no voice. Voxtral, next, brings the voice path.

These are the terms the paper uses without explaining. The most important are pixel shuffle, which cuts visual tokens by the square of its ratio, the context window, which is how many tokens the model can read at once, and SigLIP and SmolLM2, the vision encoder and language model inside SmolVLM. The benchmark names at the end, such as OCRBench, MMMU and Video-MME, appear in the results table.

Voxtral asks how to give a text language model good ears without hurting what it already knows. Mistral's answer is simple: put a Whisper speech encoder in front of a Mistral decoder, compress the audio four times with a small adapter, and train on audio and text together. The tab starts with the big picture of every input path, then the problems of long audio and synthetic speech, the method and training recipe, the few relations the paper states in prose, all nine figures redrawn, the eight tables, and finally a box on using Voxtral in your own project. In the atlas this is the first paper of the hearing group. It comes after QLoRA, TinyLLaVA Factory and SmolVLM, which cover fine-tuning and vision, and before Voxtral Realtime, LFM2 and the omni models that combine all three senses.

Voxtral has two working inputs and one output. Read the drawing left to right: indigo is the text path and the Mistral decoder, gold is the audio path through the Whisper encoder, magenta is the adapter that shrinks audio four times, and grey dashed boxes are inputs and outputs that simply do not exist. Images and video have no encoder, and the model never speaks. This is the picture to keep in mind when you plan which inputs a model takes natively.

Long audio is the core engineering problem. Each bar is the number of tokens a recording would need, and the dashed indigo line is the 32 thousand token context. At the Whisper rate of 50 frames per second, thirty minutes is 90 thousand tokens and does not fit. At 12.5 per second, forty minutes is 30 thousand and fits. The adapter in the method section exists to make this possible.

Cheap synthetic speech has a hidden cost. Turning text instructions into speech with a text to speech voice is an easy way to build spoken training data, but a model trained only on it often transcribes a real, accented question instead of answering it. The paper's fix is to add genuine human questions cut from long speech recordings. Keep this in mind if you plan to build your spoken dataset with a speech synthesizer.

Audio becomes tokens in four moves: chunk, encode, concatenate, compress. The whole clip becomes one log Mel spectrogram, which is cut into 30 second windows, with the last one padded. Each window goes through Whisper on its own with positional encodings reset, the outputs are joined, and the magenta adapter merges every four frames into one token. So every 30 seconds of sound costs 375 tokens in the language model.

The training schedule starts by warming up only the bridge. Rust cells are trained and grey cells are frozen. In the first pass only the adapter learns, with Whisper and the language model frozen, and the paper found this helps speech understanding. For the later phases the paper does not say which modules stay frozen, so those cells are dashed. For your QLoRA run this is useful evidence that training the adapter alone already connects audio to text.

The recipe has five stages that move from alignment to behaviour. First, long recordings are split into matched audio and text pieces. Then a warm up trains only the adapter. Pretraining mixes two patterns half and half, one teaching transcription and one teaching the model to carry context across speech and text. Supervised fine-tuning adds question answering, spoken instructions and a transcribe mode. Preference alignment with DPO finally polishes the answers.

Most instruction data is synthetic but anchored in real audio. The top row shows a large language model reading transcripts and writing listening questions, summaries and translations. The middle row turns text instructions into speech with a synthetic voice. The bottom row adds real human spoken questions answered from world knowledge. The magenta transcribe mode token lets the model do speech recognition with no text prompt. This is a practical template for building your own three hundred training examples.

A text judge can grade audio answers. The current model samples two answers at temperature 0.5, the audio is replaced by its transcript, and a text reward model picks the better answer. The DPO update then pushes the model toward it, and the loop repeats with fresh samples, which is what makes it online. The paper reports that the online version helped more than offline DPO, as Table 2 shows.

Mistral built new benchmarks by turning text tests into speech. An LLM first sorts each question from GSM8K, TriviaQA and MMLU into speakable, speakable after rewriting, or unspeakable. The rewrite rules are really text normalization: numbers become words, acronyms are spelled out and markdown is removed. A synthetic voice then reads each question with a randomly chosen speaker. These rules are a ready checklist for a text normalization experiment.

The internal speech understanding benchmark is scored by an LLM judge that never hears the audio. For every answer, the judge reads the transcript, the question, a reference answer and the candidate. It gives a one or zero for correct and helpful, and a grade from zero to five. Each answer is judged ten times and the mean and standard deviation are reported. Table 2 uses exactly these two scores.

label: (u1)
text: Audio moves through three frame rates. The log Mel spectrogram, with a hop of 160 samples, has 100 frames per second. Whisper's convolution stem halves that to 50, and the MLP adapter divides by four to reach 12.5 audio tokens per second. The paper states the 50 and 12.5 values; the 100 follows from Whisper's 16 kilohertz input. Figure 8 is the experiment that justifies stopping at 12.5.

label: (u2)
text: The number of audio tokens is simply the frame rate r times the duration t in seconds. Thirty minutes at 50 per second gives 90 thousand tokens, far beyond the context. Forty minutes at 12.5 per second gives 30 thousand, which fits under 32 thousand 768. This one line is the reason the adapter exists, and you can use the same arithmetic to budget memory for your own clips.

label: (u3)
text: Every clip is padded up to the next multiple of 30 seconds, and the number of chunks is the duration divided by 30, rounded up. Each chunk becomes 375 audio tokens. So a five second voice question still costs a full 375 tokens, which matters for GPU memory on a free T4. Figure 7 tests whether this padding could be dropped, and the answer was no.

label: (u4)
text: The repetition pattern is a speech recognition lesson. A training sequence starts with a begin token, then the audio segment A n, then the repeat token, then its own transcript T n, and an end token. The model learns to write down exactly what it heard. Figure 9 shows that this pattern alone gives low word error rates but almost no question answering ability.

label: (u5)
text: The continuation pattern alternates modalities: audio one, then text two, then audio three, then text four, and so on. Each audio segment is followed by the next piece of text rather than its own transcript, marked by the next token. This teaches the model to keep a conversation going across speech and text. Half of pretraining uses this pattern and half uses repetition.

label: (u6)
text: The training objective is ordinary next token prediction on text. The loss is minus the sum of the log probabilities of each text token y i, given the earlier tokens, the audio tokens a and the text prompt x. The paper does not print this formula, but Figure 1 describes exactly this. Your LoRA fine-tuning uses the same loss, usually computed only on the answer tokens.

label: (bg)
text: DPO is background here; the paper cites it but does not print it. The loss compares how much the model, relative to a frozen reference, prefers the chosen answer y w over the rejected answer y l, scaled by beta and passed through a sigmoid. Minimising it makes good answers more likely without training a separate reward model. In Voxtral's online variant, both answers are fresh samples from the current model.

label: (u7)
text: The parameter budget adds four parts: the 640 million parameter Whisper encoder, the small adapter, the text embedding table and the decoder. Voxtral Mini totals about 4.7 billion and Small about 24.3 billion. The encoder is the same in both, and the adapter is under one percent of the total. For your GPU budget, Mini is the one to consider.
