text: Voxtral Small leads every translation direction on FLEURS. Bars show BLEU, where higher is better, for four directions out of English and four into English. Small, in magenta, is on top in all eight. Gemini 2.5 Flash drops sharply when translating into English. Mini sits close to GPT 4o mini Audio for translation into English, which is good for a much smaller model.

label: Fig. 5
text: On spoken question answering Voxtral competes but does not win. Bars are accuracy on seven tasks, some real speech and some synthesized from text benchmarks. Voxtral Small beats GPT 4o mini Audio on three tasks, while Gemini 2.5 Flash leads most. Mini falls far behind on knowledge tasks like MMLU, yet scores 85.6 on the internal benchmark. Knowledge is limited by the small 3 billion parameter decoder, not by hearing.

label: Fig. 6
text: Adding ears barely costs text skill. Each group is a text-only benchmark; gold is Mini, magenta is Small and indigo is its text-only parent, Mistral Small 3.1. Small stays within a few points of its parent everywhere, with the largest gap on GSM8K math. The values are read from the plot and are approximate. Mixing text data into pretraining is what protects these scores.

label: Fig. 7a
text: Padding hardly matters for English. The chart tracks word error rate on FLEURS English during training, for a run that pads audio to 30 seconds in magenta and a run that does not in dashed gold. Both end near the same value. This panel alone would suggest dropping padding, but the French panel next to it changes the decision. The curve shapes are redrawn, not exact.

label: Fig. 7b
text: French is where removing padding hurts. The padded run in magenta ends lower than the unpadded run in dashed gold, a gap of about half a word error rate point. Whisper was pretrained on padded 30 second windows, and even fine-tuning the encoder did not fully adapt it. That is why Voxtral keeps the padding. The curve shapes are redrawn, not exact.

label: Fig. 7c
text: Understanding does not depend on padding. Three shot accuracy on Llama QA rises from about 40 to over 50 percent for both runs, and the two lines cross several times. Taken together, the three panels of Figure 7 say padding costs nothing in understanding and helps transcription, so it stays. The curve shapes are redrawn, not exact.

label: Fig. 8a
text: The English test cannot tell the frame rates apart. Four runs downsample Whisper output to 50, 25, 12.5 and 6.25 frames per second, and all end close together in word error rate. The chosen 12.5 hertz run is in magenta. The next two panels decide the question. The curve shapes are redrawn, not exact.

label: Fig. 8b
text: Too much compression hurts French transcription. The 6.25 hertz run, in dashed rust, stays more than one word error rate point above the others, while 25 and 12.5 hertz end close to the uncompressed 50 hertz run. So eight times compression is too much and four times is safe. The curve shapes are redrawn, not exact.

label: Fig. 8c
text: Compression can even help understanding. On Llama QA the 12.5 hertz run, in magenta, ends about 1.5 points above the 50 hertz baseline. The authors suggest that at 12.5 per second one audio token carries about as much information as one text token, which suits the language model. This is the evidence behind the magenta adapter in the big picture. The curve shapes are redrawn, not exact.

label: Fig. 9a
text: Without repetition data the model cannot transcribe. Word error rate on three shot FLEURS English is plotted for three pretraining mixes. Repetition only, in indigo, and the half and half mix, in magenta, stay near five percent, while continuation only, in dashed gold, jumps between about 50 and 80 percent. The curve shapes are redrawn, not exact.

label: Fig. 9b
text: French tells the same story as English. The repetition only and half and half mixes stay below ten percent word error rate, while continuation only stays far higher. The repetition pattern is what teaches exact speech to text mapping. The curve shapes are redrawn, not exact.

label: Fig. 9c
text: Without continuation data the model cannot answer questions. On Llama QA, repetition only in indigo stays near zero accuracy, while the half and half mix and continuation only both climb above 50 percent. Together with the two panels before it, this proves the balanced mix gets both skills at once. The curve shapes are redrawn, not exact.

Almost all of Voxtral's size is the language decoder. The table splits each model into the audio encoder, adapter, text embeddings and decoder. The encoder is the same 640 million parameters in both variants, and the adapter is only 25 or 52 million. Mini has 4.7 billion parameters in total and Small has 24.3 billion. This tells you where LoRA adapters will matter most: in the decoder.

Preference tuning improves answers but can cost transcription. The table gives the judge's helpfulness percentage, the zero to five grade and English word error rate, each judged ten times. Online DPO gives the best helpfulness for both sizes, but for Small the word error rate rises from 6.31 to 6.50. That is why Mistral released the Online DPO checkpoint for Mini but kept the plain fine-tuned checkpoint for Small.

Preference tuning adds about two points of judged helpfulness. Bars show the judge score for each checkpoint; the rust colour marks what the preference stage changed. Mini rises from 83.5 to 85.6 and Small from 86.6 to 88.3, close to Gemini 2.5 Flash at 88.6. Standard deviations are one to four points, so small gaps between neighbouring bars should be read with care.

English transcription is broken down by dataset here. Lower word error rate is better, and the best value in each column is highlighted. Voxtral Small is best on LibriSpeech and SPGISpeech, but Gemini wins SwitchBoard, a telephone conversation dataset, and Scribe wins CHiME 4 noise and the long earnings calls. Conversational and noisy speech remain harder, which is useful context for your error analysis.

FLEURS word error rates by language reveal big differences. English, Spanish and Italian are around two to four percent, while Arabic and Hindi are much higher. Voxtral Mini's Arabic error rate is 25.4, against 3.8 for English. Voxtral Small is best on French and German. This table is the source for the Arabic and English fairness comparison in the chart below.

Common Voice shows the same language gap, only larger. Common Voice is read speech from volunteers, with varied microphones and accents. Arabic word error rate is above 45 percent for every model and above 60 for all Voxtral variants, which is why the paper leaves Arabic out of the Figure 3 average. Leaving a group out of an average like this is itself a fairness question worth discussing in your report.

Multilingual LibriSpeech adds read audiobooks in six European languages. Voxtral Small or Mini Transcribe is best in four of six columns, with Gemini best on Dutch and GPT 4o mini Transcribe best on German. Scribe does badly on Dutch at 38 percent, a reminder that one model can be strong on one dataset and weak on another. The paper does not plot this table.

Translation scores are listed per language direction. Higher BLEU is better. Voxtral Small is best in all eight columns, from 39.9 into Spanish and Italian up to 57.3 into French. Whisper can only translate into English, so its first four cells are empty. These are the exact numbers behind Figure 4.

Speech understanding scores behind Figure 5 are listed per task. The starred columns are text benchmarks read aloud by a synthetic voice. Gemini 2.5 Flash is best on six of seven tasks, and GPT 4o mini Audio on Llama QA. Voxtral Small is competitive, and Mini scores well only on the in-house benchmark. Note that the table calls it AU Bench, while the figure calls it SU benchmark.

Arabic is Voxtral's weak spot, and that gives you a ready fairness experiment. Bars compare word error rate on Arabic and English for the three Voxtral models on two datasets. On FLEURS, Mini's Arabic error of 25.4 is almost seven times its English 3.8; on Common Voice, Arabic is above 60 percent for all three. A bigger decoder and transcription-only training shrink the gap but do not close it.

Use this box as the plan for your project. Voxtral handles your voice and text inputs natively, so the only extra piece is a small vision model that turns the image into text. Start from Voxtral Mini in four bit, put LoRA on the decoder projections, keep Whisper frozen, and check memory with 30 second padded clips on a T4. Build the dataset the way the paper did, with some real human recordings, and use Arabic against English as your fairness split.

label: Primer
text: Sound reaches the language model in four steps. The waveform becomes a log-Mel spectrogram, a picture of sound with a hundred frames per second. The Whisper encoder turns it into fifty vectors per second, and Voxtral's adapter merges every four into one audio token, so twelve and a half per second. Those gold audio tokens and the indigo text tokens form one sequence, and the decoder reads them like words.

label: Primer
text: Word error rate is the paper's main score for transcription, and a natural metric for your base versus fine-tuned comparison. Line up the output with the reference, count substitutions, deletions and insertions, and divide by the number of reference words. Here three mistakes over six words give fifty percent. Notice that writing ten instead of the digits removes one error, which is exactly why your normalization experiment matters.

label: Primer
text: This is a sensible fine-tuning plan for a small project, not a recipe printed in the paper. Grey parts stay frozen: the six hundred and forty million parameter Whisper encoder and the decoder, stored in four bits. Rust parts learn: LoRA adapters on the decoder's attention and MLP layers, and optionally the small twenty five million parameter adapter, which the paper itself trains alone in its warm-up stage.

label: Primer
text: Voxtral is paper four of eleven in the atlas. SmolVLM before it adds sight, reading images and answering in text. Voxtral adds hearing, taking speech and text in and giving text out, with up to forty minutes of audio. The image chip is grey, so for a text, image and voice task you need a small vision model beside it. Voxtral Realtime, next, turns the same idea into live, streaming transcription.

These are the words the paper uses without explaining them. Read log-Mel spectrogram, adapter and context window first, because they explain how audio fits into a language model. WER and BLEU are the scores in the results tables, FLEURS and Common Voice are the speech test sets, and TTS, diarization and DPO describe how the training data and preference tuning were built.

Voxtral Realtime asks whether a speech recognizer can write text while you are still talking and still be as accurate as a model that waits for the whole recording. Its answer is yes: a 4.4 billion parameter model with a causal audio encoder and a language decoder that emits one token every 80 milliseconds, matching offline Whisper at a delay of 480 milliseconds. The tab moves from the big picture and the problem to the method, the equations, all five figures, the eight results tables, and a box on what this means for your own project. When choosing models, remember the short version: it hears speech and writes text, and nothing else. Among the eleven papers in this atlas it sits in the hearing group, right after Voxtral and before LFM2. It follows QLoRA, TinyLLaVA Factory and SmolVLM, and the omni models later in the atlas take the same audio ideas further.

Only one input path exists here, the gold audio path. Speech at 16 kilohertz becomes a log Mel spectrogram, passes a causal convolution and a 32 layer causal encoder, and an adapter squeezes it to one embedding every 80 milliseconds. That embedding is added to the model's own previous text token, and the decoder writes the next token, guided by the delay tau in magenta. The grey boxes are what it cannot do: images, video, text instructions and speech output.

The core problem is a mismatch between training and use. An offline recognizer like Whisper learns while looking at the whole utterance, including the future. If you feed it chunks as they arrive, it must answer before that future exists, and the mismatch hurts most at low delay. Native streaming, on the right, trains exactly as it runs: past audio only, text lagging by a fixed delay. The three boxes below list what such a model needs, and the method section supplies each one.

This is a training problem the authors hit, drawn as a schematic because the paper gives no curves. The language model head and the text embeddings share weights, so as logits grew, text embeddings grew too while audio embeddings shrank. The decoder then trusted the text stream and ignored the sound. A z loss penalty on the softmax normalizer, equation seven, kept both norms stable. It is a useful warning whenever you mix a strong text model with a new audio input.

Here you can follow the frame rates from sound to token. Sixteen thousand samples per second become 100 Mel frames per second, the strided convolution halves that to 50, and the adapter stacks four encoder frames into one decoder input, giving 12.5 steps per second, or one per 80 milliseconds. The bottom boxes show why memory stays bounded: a four frame history for the convolution, a 15 second window in the encoder, and 8192 tokens in the decoder. This explains precisely how audio enters the model.

Ada RMS-Norm is the paper's key mechanism for controlling delay. The delay tau is turned into a sinusoidal embedding, passed through a tiny MLP, and becomes a vector g of tau. Inside every decoder block, the normalised input to the feed-forward branch is multiplied by one plus g of tau, while the attention branch is left alone. That costs only about five million parameters, and it lets one model run at any delay from 80 to 2400 milliseconds. Figure 3 shows it beats the alternatives.

Training targets tell the decoder when to speak. Every 80 millisecond frame gets exactly one target token: the pad token P while it waits, then a word boundary token W once a word is complete and the delay has passed, then the word itself. The top row groups words that share an emission frame under one W, so Mistral is stays normal text. The bottom row, with a W before every word, breaks that pattern. Figure 4 shows grouping trains far faster.

The recipe protects the pretrained decoder before training everything. Rust boxes are trained in that phase and grey means frozen. For the first five percent, the new encoder and adapter learn while the Ministral 3B decoder stays frozen, so random audio features cannot damage it. Then everything trains together at a lower learning rate. Delay sampling and the z loss run throughout. Note that this is full training on a huge corpus, not LoRA.

The procedure has a clear logic. First turn transcripts with word timestamps into frame by frame targets, so audio and text are aligned. Then give each example a random delay so one model learns them all. Initialise the decoder from a pretrained text model and the encoder from scratch, warm up the encoder while the decoder is frozen, and only then train end to end with a z loss. Serving comes last and adds engineering, not new learning.

This loop is our summary of how the model runs live, since the paper has no algorithm box. After a short prefill of silence and the first tau milliseconds of audio, every 80 milliseconds the encoder and adapter turn new sound into one embedding. It is added to the previous token, the decoder outputs one token, and only real subword tokens go to the transcript. The chosen token is fed back as the next step's text input, which is exactly the resumable request of Figure 5.

The encoder runs at 50 hertz and the decoder at 12.5, so each decoder step adds four encoder cache positions. Standard paged attention in vLLM assumes one position per step, which would break the indexing. The authors stretch the encoder block size and slot mapping by four, drawn here as each indigo decoder slot fanning out to four gold encoder slots. This is serving engineering; you only need it if you deploy the model live.

label: (i)
text: This is the first half of every decoder block. The hidden state x is normalised with RMS norm, passed through attention, and the result r attn is added back to x to give h. Nothing about the delay enters here. The paper keeps the attention branch unconditioned on purpose, and the next equation shows where the delay goes instead.

label: (ii)
text: This is the second half of the block and the heart of Ada RMS-Norm. The normalised h is multiplied element by element by one plus g of tau before the feed-forward network, and its output r f f n is added back to give y. If g of tau were zero, you would get an ordinary transformer block, so the delay acts as a gentle, learned rescaling of each feature.

label: (iii)
text: This writes out in symbols what the paper says in words. The delay tau is encoded with sine and cosine waves, then a small MLP with a GELU activation and an inner width of only 32 maps it to a vector of size d, 3072 for this decoder. That vector is g of tau, used in equation two. The narrow inner width is why the whole mechanism adds only about five million parameters.

label: (iv)
text: During training the delay is drawn uniformly from thirty values, 80 milliseconds times k, for k from one to thirty, so from 80 up to 2400 milliseconds. Each value is a whole number of 80 millisecond adapter frames. Because the model sees all of them, one set of weights can serve any of those delays at inference, which is what the latency curve in Figure 1 sweeps.

label: (v)
text: This line is just the frame rate arithmetic. Sixteen thousand samples per second divided by a hop of 160 gives 100 Mel frames per second; the strided convolution halves that to 50; the adapter divides by four to reach 12.5 per second, which is one step every 80 milliseconds. The encoder window of 750 frames at 50 per second covers 15 seconds. Use these numbers when you explain the audio path of a model.

label: (vi)
text: RMS norm is the standard normalisation used throughout the model, written out here because the paper only names it. Each feature is divided by the root mean square of all d features, plus a small epsilon for safety, then scaled by a learned gain gamma. Unlike layer norm it does not subtract the mean. Ada RMS-Norm in equation two simply adds a delay dependent scale on top of this.

label: (vii)
text: The z loss is added to the usual cross entropy. Z is the softmax normaliser, the sum of the exponentials of all logits, and the penalty lambda times log Z squared pushes log Z toward zero, so logits cannot grow without bound. The paper names this loss but gives neither the formula nor lambda, so this is the standard form from PaLM. It solves the norm drift shown in the problem section.

label: (viii)
text: Word error rate is the metric in every table, and you will likely use it in your own evaluation. Count the substituted, deleted and inserted words needed to turn the model output into the reference, and divide by the number of reference words. Character error rate does the same over characters, used for Chinese and Japanese. Your score depends heavily on text normalisation, which makes it a useful experiment to run.

label: Fig. 1
text: The headline result in one chart. The magenta line is Voxtral Realtime's average word error rate on the 13 language FLEURS benchmark as the delay grows, on a log scale: 10.8 percent at 240 milliseconds, 8.72 at 480, 7.70 at 960 and 6.73 at 2400. The flat lines are baselines: Scribe v2 Realtime at 8.34, offline Whisper at 8.23, and Mistral's offline model at 5.90. The streaming model crosses Whisper between half a second and one second of delay.

label: Fig. 2
text: This is the paper's own picture of the model, redrawn. Read it bottom up. Audio enters the causal encoder and adapter, giving one gold embedding A per 80 millisecond frame. Each is added to the previous token and the decoder predicts the next token. It writes P while the word Mistral is still being spoken, then W, Mistral and is, waits again, then W and building. The dashed lines show each output becoming the next input.

label: Fig. 3
text: This ablation compares three ways to tell the model the delay, on English, French and German during training. Grey is summing a delay embedding with the input, as DSM does. Dashed is special delay tokens in the text. Magenta is Ada RMS-Norm, which sits lowest nearly all the way. The curves are redrawn from the plot, so read shapes, not exact values, and note the axis is really a fraction, not a percent. It justifies equation two.

label: Fig. 4
text: This ablation tests the target format from the method section. The dashed line puts a W token before every word; the magenta line uses one W per group of words that share an emission frame. Grouping is far better from early on, for example about 0.13 against 0.36 in English at five percent of training. The reason is that grouping keeps the text sequences the decoder learned in pretraining. Values are redrawn approximately.

label: Fig. 5
text: Figure 5 shows how a live session runs in vLLM. The first request carries a start token, padding tokens and the first buffered audio, 560 milliseconds in the example, and decodes one token, Hello. Each later request sends 80 more milliseconds of audio plus the token just produced, and the engine reuses its cached keys and values to produce the next token. Input and output stream at the same time, which is what makes the delay real in practice.

This chart turns Table 3 into bars. For each benchmark group, grey is offline Whisper and the magenta bars are Voxtral Realtime at four delays, darker meaning longer delay. Every group improves as delay grows. At 480 milliseconds the model roughly matches Whisper on English and FLEURS, and at 960 it beats Whisper everywhere. Common Voice is the hardest set for all models, a hint that crowd recorded speech is tougher.

Accuracy is not shared equally across languages. For each of the 13 FLEURS languages, grey is Whisper and magenta is Voxtral Realtime at 480 milliseconds. Arabic is the worst for the streaming model, 22.5 percent against 4.9 for English, while Hindi improves a lot over Whisper. For a fairness check in your own evaluation, this is a ready made comparison between Arabic and English input.

Table 1 gives the model's exact size. The audio encoder has 32 layers of width 1280 and 970 million parameters. The adapter is a single MLP that maps four stacked 1280 wide frames to 3072, only 25 million parameters. The language decoder has 26 layers, grouped query attention with 32 heads and 8 key value heads, and 3.4 billion parameters. The total is 4.4 billion, which matters when you check whether it fits a free Colab GPU.

Table 2 contrasts this encoder with Whisper's. Whisper attends both ways, uses layer norm, GELU and sinusoidal positions over a fixed 30 second window. Voxtral Realtime's encoder is causal, with RMS norm, SwiGLU, rotary positions and a sliding window, and it is larger, 970 million against 640 million parameters. Causality is the change that makes streaming possible; the rest are modern design choices.

Table 3 is the main result. It gives average word error rates for English short form, English long form, FLEURS and Common Voice, for offline models, commercial realtime services and open streaming models. Voxtral Realtime at 2400 milliseconds is the best realtime model on three of the four groups, and even at 480 it beats the other open streaming systems, DSM and Nemotron. Dashes mean the model does not support those languages.

Table 4 tests a free trick: padding the start of the stream with silent frames and matching pad tokens. This does not add delay, only a bigger first step. Going from zero to 16 frames helps everywhere, most on long English audio, where error falls from about 11 to 7.9 percent. Thirty two frames helps a little more except on Common Voice. The authors suspect the padding acts like attention sinks. The rows match the 480 millisecond results, though the paper does not say so.

Table 5 breaks English short form results into ten test sets, from clean audiobooks in LibriSpeech to phone calls in Switchboard and CallHome, noisy CHiME-4 and earnings calls. Error varies hugely with recording conditions, from under 2 percent on clean LibriSpeech to over 13 percent on phone speech. Voxtral Realtime improves steadily with delay on almost every set.

Table 6 covers long English recordings, including ten minute segments of earnings calls. Long audio is where Nemotron Streaming struggles, above 13 percent error, while Voxtral Realtime stays close to offline quality, 7.73 percent at 480 milliseconds and 6.93 at 2400, the best average in the table. The sliding windows in the encoder and decoder are what make such long streams possible.

Table 7 lists FLEURS error rates for all 13 languages, character error rate for Chinese and Japanese. Look at the Arabic column: 22.53 percent for Voxtral Realtime at 480 milliseconds, against 4.90 for English. Longer delay helps every language, and Arabic most, down to 14.71 at 2400. These per language numbers are the source for the fairness chart and for your own Arabic versus English comparison.

Table 8 repeats the per language comparison on Mozilla Common Voice, which is crowd recorded and harder. Every model is above 45 percent error on Arabic, so the authors leave Arabic out of the averages. That exclusion is itself a fairness point worth discussing in your report. Voxtral Realtime at 2400 milliseconds has the best realtime average, 10.47 percent.

Use this box to plan your project. Voxtral Realtime only hears speech and writes text, so for a text, image and voice task treat it as the speech to text stage and send its transcript and the image to a small vision language model that you fine tune with QLoRA. It comes in one 4.4 billion parameter size; check library and memory support before trying to fine tune it on a T4, because its training data also needs word timestamps. Choose a long delay for offline work, and use Arabic versus English for your fairness experiment.

label: Primer
text: Streaming means the model writes while you are still talking. The gold row is the speaker, the indigo rows are two kinds of recognizer. An offline model such as Whisper waits for the whole clip, then writes everything. A streaming model writes each word a fixed delay, called tau, after it is spoken, shown here as 480 milliseconds. A short delay feels live but gives the model less evidence, and that trade-off is the whole story of this paper.

label: Primer
text: Speech reaches the language model in four steps. The waveform, sixteen thousand samples a second, becomes a log-Mel spectrogram at a hundred frames a second. A causal encoder turns that into fifty vectors a second, each built only from sound already heard, and an adapter stacks four of them into one vector every 80 milliseconds. The decoder then writes exactly one token per step: a wait token, or a word marker followed by the word.

label: Primer
text: Word error rate counts how many edits turn the model's transcript into the reference. Here one word is substituted, one deleted and one inserted, out of six reference words, so the rate is three over six, or fifty percent. Lower is better. Every table in the paper uses this metric, and you will likely use it too. Remember that capital letters and punctuation count as errors unless you normalize both texts first.

label: Primer
text: This is paper five of eleven,. Voxtral, the previous paper, taught a Mistral language model to listen, but only to finished recordings. Voxtral Realtime keeps the same 80 millisecond audio rate and adds live transcription with a delay you choose. It accepts voice only, with no image and no text prompt. LFM2, next, moves to fast small backbones with image and audio variants. For your task, treat it as the speech to text stage of a pipeline.

These are the words the paper uses without explaining. The most important are delay, which is how far the transcript lags behind the voice, causal attention, which means looking only at the past, and word error rate, the score in every table. FLEURS and Common Voice are the two multilingual test sets, and Whisper is the offline baseline the paper tries to match. Come back here whenever a term in the tab stops you.

The LFM2 report asks how to build small language models that run fast on phones and laptop processors while still being good at real tasks. Its answer is a minimal hybrid backbone: mostly cheap gated short convolutions with only a few attention layers, chosen by measuring speed on the actual devices, plus careful distillation and post-training. On top of that backbone it builds LFM2-VL for images and LFM2-Audio for speech, which is why it matters for multimodal fine-tuning. The tab starts with the big picture of all input paths, then the problems, the method for the backbone and both multimodal variants, every equation and figure, the result tables, and a box on how to put it into practice. In the atlas it is the sixth of eleven papers, after the two Voxtral speech papers and before the omni models, starting with MiniMind-O.

This is the map for the whole paper. Read each row from left to right: text in indigo, images in teal, speech in gold, all ending as vectors that enter the same LFM2 backbone in the middle. The magenta block is the new idea, the gated short convolution. Notice that video is crossed out and that no single model uses all three rows, so a text plus image plus voice task needs two models or a speech-to-text step.

Here is why attention in every layer hurts on a phone. Each bar is the memory needed to keep keys and values for a thirty-two thousand token context, computed from Table 1. Keeping attention in only six of sixteen layers cuts the cache to about three eighths, and the convolution layers add almost nothing because they only remember the last two positions. This is the memory problem the hybrid backbone solves.

This schematic shows the second problem, which is about training rather than inference. The teacher stores only its top thirty-two probabilities per token. If you then apply a temperature over the whole vocabulary, the rust curve keeps growing with the square of the temperature, because teacher and student no longer cover the same tokens. The magenta decoupled loss stays bounded. There are no measured values here; it only shows the shape of the argument in Appendix A.

The architecture was not designed by hand but searched with the hardware in the loop. Read it as a cycle: candidates from the search space are scored for quality on more than fifty evaluations and timed on a real phone and laptop, then filtered on a three-way Pareto front of quality, latency and memory. The loop kept returning the same answer, the magenta outcome: mostly gated short convolutions and a few attention layers, with no state-space or linear-attention blocks.

These four steps are the search procedure in order. First define what counts as good: quality, latency and peak memory. Then list every building block the search may use, from sliding-window attention to Mamba. Then compile each candidate with the same quantized runtimes the company ships and time it on the target devices. Finally throw away anything over budget and keep the Pareto survivors. The key lesson is to optimize the real objective, not a proxy like perplexity.

This is the operator that makes LFM2 fast. One linear layer makes three streams called B, C and h tilde. B multiplies h tilde element by element, a three-tap depthwise convolution mixes each channel with its two previous positions, C gates the result, and an output linear layer projects back. The inset on the right shows the payoff at decode time: a convolution layer keeps two past steps, while an attention layer keeps keys and values for every past token.

The pseudo-code restates the same block as runnable steps, since the paper gives it only as one line of math. The first function is the gated short convolution; the second is a full layer, with pre-norm, a residual connection around the sequence block, and another around the feedforward block. The sequence block is either the convolution or grouped-query attention. When you add LoRA in your own project, the two linear layers in the first function are natural targets.

The hyperparameter table tells you the exact layout of each size. The three smallest models have sixteen layers, of which six are attention and ten are convolution blocks; the 2.6 billion model has thirty layers with eight attention. All use eight key-value groups with head size sixty-four and a convolution kernel of three. The mixture-of-experts model has thirty-two experts per layer and activates four per token, which is why only 1.5 billion of its 8.3 billion parameters run per token.

Decoupled distillation in one picture. On the left, the teacher's probabilities, where only the top thirty-two indigo bars are stored. The loss splits into two parts: the upper box asks whether the student puts the same total probability into those top tokens, with no temperature; the lower box compares the renormalized shape inside the set, where temperature is applied. This is exactly equations one and two, and it fixes the problem shown earlier.

Post-training turns the pretrained model into an assistant in three stages. Supervised fine-tuning uses about five million filtered, deduplicated samples ordered from easy to hard by how many of twelve reference models solve them. Preference alignment samples five answers per prompt, lets an LLM jury pick the best and worst, and trains with a length-normalized loss. Model merging then combines the best candidates. The curriculum idea is simple enough to reuse in your own fine-tuning data.

This table shows what the supervised fine-tuning data is made of. For the dense models, general-purpose chat, instruction following and retrieval-augmented generation make up more than half, and math is only about seven percent. The mixture-of-experts model shifts heavily toward math at twenty-six percent and adds code. The letters show the source: proprietary, licensed or open-source. It explains why the dense models are strong at instruction following and the MoE model at math.

These are the settings for the preference-alignment stage. Beta, the KL coefficient that scales the implicit reward in equation five, is five. The learning rate is tiny, peaking at eight times ten to the minus seven with cosine decay, the batch is two thousand and forty-eight, context is one thousand and twenty-four tokens, and training runs for two epochs. Small learning rates like this are typical when you only nudge an already fine-tuned model.

A diamond decides the route: images up to five hundred and twelve by five hundred and twelve pixels are resized once; larger ones are cut into two to ten tiles plus an optional thumbnail. SigLIP2 encodes patches, then PixelUnshuffle folds each two by two group into one wider vector, cutting tokens by four, and an MLP maps them to the language model width. The result is between about one hundred and twenty-eight and two thousand eight hundred visual tokens.

This grid shows which parts are trained in each stage, which is the most practical diagram for your fine-tuning. Rust cells are trained, grey cells frozen, dashed cells are trained but the paper does not say so explicitly. Both LFM2-VL and LFM2-Audio first train only the small connector with the encoder and backbone frozen, then unfreeze everything. It is the same idea as training only a few added parameters with LoRA first.

The vision model first aligns the connector on captions, then trains everything with the vision encoder at one fifth of the learning rate, then does supervised fine-tuning with tiling on and five to thirty percent image samples. The audio model aligns the connector on speech recognition data, then mid-trains on about one hundred billion tokens. Losses are only on discrete outputs, text tokens and speech codes, never on the continuous audio inputs.

LFM2-Audio speaks in real time like this. For each eighty-millisecond frame the big backbone runs once, then a small one hundred and fifteen million parameter RQ-Transformer runs eight quick steps to produce the eight codebook codes. In interleaved mode, six text tokens are followed by twelve audio tokens, so the words are decided before they are spoken. Sequential mode switches between a text state and an audio state with special tokens, which is how speech recognition and text-to-speech work.

The pseudo-code turns the interleaved schedule into a loop. The model alternates six text tokens with twelve audio frames, and each audio frame is one backbone step plus eight depth-decoder steps whose code embeddings are summed and fed back. When the text ends, the model keeps producing audio until it emits the end-of-audio code. If you ever use LFM2-Audio for spoken answers, this is the loop your library runs for you.

The audio data table shows the scale behind LFM2-Audio. Per epoch there are about thirteen billion text tokens, one hundred and forty-six thousand hours of input speech and three hundred and twenty-six thousand hours of output speech, mostly from audio chat instruction tuning. That is about four hundred and seventy-two thousand hours in total, close to Whisper's six hundred and eighty thousand. A few hundred training examples are tiny by comparison, which is exactly why LoRA is the right tool.

This diagram covers the retrieval variant, LFM2-ColBERT. Each query token, on the left, is compared with every document token; the magenta cell in each row is the best match, and the score adds these row maxima. Documents can be encoded in advance and indexed, which keeps search fast. It is not needed for a text, image and voice task, but it shows how the same backbone is reused for a very different task.

This equation is the gated short convolution written compactly. A linear layer turns the hidden sequence h into three parts, B, C and h tilde. Then y equals B times h tilde element-wise, z is a depthwise convolution of y with kernel size k, and the output o is a linear layer applied to C times z. It is the formula behind the block diagram in the method section.

These definitions prepare the distillation loss. P T of the set T is the total probability the teacher gives to its top-K tokens for a context x c. The second part renormalizes the teacher distribution inside that set so it sums to one. The same definitions hold for the student, P S. Equations one and two are built from these two quantities.

This defines temperature. Raising every probability to the power one over tau and renormalizing flattens the distribution when tau is larger than one. The tempered KL divergence is multiplied by tau squared so the gradient size stays comparable across temperatures. The paper applies this only inside the top-K set, which is the whole point of the decoupled method.

Equation one is the first half of the distillation loss, L B. It is a KL divergence between two coin flips: the teacher's probability that the next token falls in its top-K set, and the student's probability of the same event. It teaches the student how much mass belongs in the top set, and it is left untempered.

Equation two is the second half, L T. It compares teacher and student inside the top-K set after renormalizing both, with temperature applied, and weights the result by the teacher's top-K mass. It teaches the relative ranking of the likely tokens. Together with equation one it forms the decoupled Top-K objective, which is then added to ordinary cross-entropy on the true next token.

This short formula defines difficulty for the curriculum. For item i, r i j is one if model j answered correctly and zero otherwise, and p i is the average over twelve models. A high p i means an easy item. The training set is sorted from easy to hard using a predictor of p i, a trick you could copy when ordering your own fine-tuning examples.

Equation three is a general recipe for preference training. Given a prompt x, a chosen answer y w and a rejected answer y l, it combines a relative term, how much more the model prefers the chosen answer minus a margin m, weighted by omega, with an absolute term weighted by lambda. The functions f and g pick the exact variant, as the special cases below show.

Equation four defines the two ingredients of the preference loss. Delta is the difference between the chosen and rejected rewards, each divided by its answer length in tokens. Small delta is the difference of their sigmoids. Dividing by length stops the model from learning that longer answers are automatically better.

Equation five is the implicit reward used in direct preference optimization. It is beta times the log ratio between the probability the trained policy gives an answer and the probability the frozen reference model gives it. Beta is five here, from Table 5. A positive reward means the model now likes that answer more than before training.

These settings show that equation three contains known methods as special cases. With omega one, f equal to log sigmoid and no absolute term you get length-normalized DPO. With only the absolute term you get APO-zero. The paper also mixes both with a margin of zero point one and lambda of zero point two, which behaves like SimPO plus an anchor on probabilities.

This is the ordinary cross-entropy loss that LFM2-Audio is trained with. For each of N target tokens it takes the log of the softmax probability of the correct token y n among V choices, and averages with a minus sign. It is computed separately for text tokens and for each of the eight speech codebooks, and never for the continuous audio inputs.

This formula writes down what the paper says only in words, so treat the exact weights as our reconstruction. The eight codebook losses are averaged with weights that decay exponentially from one hundred for the first, semantic codebook to one for the last. The total loss then averages text and audio losses weighted by how many tokens of each are in the batch. Emphasizing the first codebooks improved perceived audio quality.

This arithmetic explains the audio rate. Sixteen thousand samples per second with a ten millisecond hop give one hundred log-mel frames per second, and the encoder downsamples by eight, so there are twelve and a half embeddings per second, each covering eighty milliseconds. A ten-second spoken question therefore becomes only about one hundred and twenty-five tokens for the language model.

Equation six defines the retrieval encoder. Text, either a query or a document, goes through the LFM2 backbone, and a linear layer without bias projects each token vector from one thousand and twenty-four down to one hundred and twenty-eight dimensions. Smaller vectors make the index cheaper to store and compare.

Equation seven is the MaxSim score. For every query token i, find the document token j with the highest cosine similarity, then sum these best matches over all query tokens. It lets each word of the question find its own evidence in the document, as in the diagram of the method section.

Equation eight trains the retriever by imitation. For a query with eight documents, a strong cross-encoder teacher gives relevance scores s i T, and the loss is the mean squared difference between those and the student's MaxSim scores. The paper says the score is equation two, but it means equation seven.

Equation nine is the full forward KL divergence between teacher and student over the whole vocabulary A, the sum of teacher probability times the log ratio. It is what ideal distillation would minimize, but it needs all sixty-five thousand teacher probabilities per token, which LFM2 does not store.

Equation ten splits that full KL exactly into three parts using the chain rule: a coin-flip term for being inside or outside the top-K set, a KL inside the set weighted by its mass, and a KL over the tail, T bar, weighted by the tail mass. Only the first two can be computed from stored top-K logits.

Equation eleven simply drops the tail term from equation ten. Because a KL divergence is never negative, what remains is a lower bound on the full KL. It is still untempered here; the next two equations add temperature in the safe place.

Equation twelve repeats the temperature definition from the main text, now for tau of at least one. It is applied only to the two conditional distributions inside the top-K set, never to the membership coin flip or to the weight in front.

Equation thirteen is the final decoupled Top-K objective, boxed in the paper and identical to equations one and two. The first term matches how much mass is on the top-K set; the second, tempered term matches the shape inside it. This is the distillation loss actually used in LFM2 pre-training.

Equation fourteen proves why the naive approach is unstable. As temperature grows, the tempered student becomes uniform over all tokens, while the truncated teacher becomes uniform over only the top-K. Their KL approaches the log of vocabulary size over K, and after multiplying by tau squared the loss keeps growing. Conditioning both on the top-K set removes this mismatch.

Equation fifteen is the same chain-rule split, but for the reverse KL, where the student comes first. It again produces a membership term, a term inside the top-K set and a tail term, now weighted by the student's own masses. The appendix includes it for completeness; LFM2 uses the forward version.

Equation sixteen is the computable lower bound for the reverse KL: drop the tail term and put temperature only inside the top-K term. Its weakness is that the student could lower its own top-K mass to shrink the second term, which motivates the next equation.

Equation seventeen fixes that incentive by weighting the inside-the-set term with the teacher's mass instead of the student's. It is no longer a strict bound, but in practice it stops the student from shrinking its top-K mass. Like the others, only the conditional term is tempered.

Equation eighteen is the simplest way to merge models, a model soup. The merged weights are a weighted average of several fine-tuned checkpoints, with weights summing to one, done tensor by tensor. It needs no extra training, which is why LFM2 tries several merges and keeps the best.

Equation nineteen is task arithmetic. Each fine-tuned model is turned into a task vector, its weights minus the base weights, and the merge adds a weighted sum of task vectors to the base. Note that tau here means a task vector, not a temperature. A LoRA adapter is essentially a compact task vector of this kind.

Equation twenty is TIES merging. Each task vector is trimmed to its largest entries, a majority sign is elected for every parameter, and only the entries that agree with that sign are averaged. This reduces interference when two fine-tunes push the same weight in opposite directions.

Equation twenty-one is DARE. Each entry of a task vector is dropped at random with probability p, and the survivors are divided by one minus p so the expected update stays the same. Surprisingly many entries can be dropped without hurting the merged model.

Equation twenty-two is the first half of DELLA. Instead of dropping entries uniformly, each gets a drop probability based on its magnitude rank, so small entries are dropped more often. P min is set so that the average drop rate is still p, and epsilon controls how spread out the probabilities are.

Equation twenty-three completes DELLA: drop each entry with its own probability p i and rescale survivors by one over one minus p i. LFM2 combines this with the TIES sign election. Together, equations eighteen to twenty-three are the menu of merging tricks behind the final checkpoints.

text: Figure nine compares encoding speed on a data-centre GPU, on log scales. The LFM2 retriever is two point three seven times larger than the baseline, yet its query and document throughput is the same at every batch size, about sixty sequences per second at batch one. The efficient backbone pays for its extra size.

This chart summarizes phone decode speed from Table 2. Magenta bars are LFM2 models, grey bars baselines, and dashed lines separate size groups. In almost every group LFM2 is fastest; the exception is Gemma three one billion, which decodes faster at four thousand tokens of context. Faster decode is what makes a spoken assistant feel responsive.

Table 2 gives the raw phone numbers behind the speed claim. Prefill is how fast a prompt of one or four thousand tokens is read; decode is how fast new tokens are produced. Green cells are best within each size group. LFM2 wins most cells, and the gap grows at four thousand tokens, where attention-heavy models slow down more.

Table 3 repeats the measurement on a laptop processor. Absolute speeds are several times higher than on the phone, and the pattern is similar though less one-sided: Gemma three one billion and a Granite model win some cells. The main point is that the architecture search did not overfit to one device.

Table 6 compares the smallest text models on knowledge, instruction following, math and multilingual benchmarks. Green marks the best in each row, and all scores come from the authors' own harness.

LFM2 2.6 billion and the mixture-of-experts model are competitive, strong on instruction following and math, but Qwen three four billion wins many rows. Keep in mind that the MoE model runs only 1.5 billion parameters per token, so it is cheap for its quality.

First, note that LFM2-VL handles text and images and LFM2-Audio handles text and speech, so your text plus image plus voice task needs a speech-to-text step before the vision model. Second, start with the 450 million or 1.6 billion vision model under QLoRA on the T4, in fp16. Third, put LoRA on the backbone linear layers and keep the encoders frozen. Finally, plan a language or speaker-group comparison and a normalization ablation.

text: Speed on a phone depends on what each layer must remember. The top row splits generation into prefill, where the whole prompt is read at once, and decode, one new token per step. The indigo attention row stores keys and values for every token and keeps growing. The magenta short convolution row keeps only the last two inputs. So LFM2 makes ten of its sixteen layers convolutions, and its speed tables report prefill and decode tokens per second.

label: Primer
text: A small model learns faster when it copies a big teacher's full guess. The grey teacher, an internal LFM1 seven billion model, gives a probability for every one of about sixty five thousand tokens. LFM2 keeps only the thirty two largest, the magenta bars, and trains the rust student to match them while still predicting the true next token. Section three of the paper is about making this Top-K trick stable. You will not need it for LoRA.

label: Primer
text: LFM2-Audio listens with continuous vectors and speaks with discrete codes. Top row: sixteen kilohertz sound becomes a log-mel spectrogram, a FastConformer encoder turns it into one vector every eighty milliseconds, and those enter the indigo backbone like words. Bottom row: a small RQ-Transformer predicts eight Mimi codec codes per frame, and a detokenizer turns them into twenty four kilohertz speech. For a text, image and voice project, the listening half is the part you would use for spoken questions.

label: Primer
text: LFM2 is paper six of eleven, between Voxtral Realtime, which transcribes live speech, and MiniMind-O, a tiny model that hears, sees and speaks. The chips show what each handles. LFM2 covers text, image and voice, but through two separate models: LFM2-VL for images and LFM2-Audio for speech. For a task that needs a photo and a spoken question together, plan a pipeline, for example LFM2-Audio for speech to text followed by LFM2-VL.

These fourteen terms are the vocabulary the report assumes. The first group is about speed on a device: prefill, decode, time to first token and the KV cache. The next covers the architecture: gated short convolution, grouped-query attention and mixture of experts. Then the inputs: SigLIP2 and PixelUnshuffle for images, log-mel, FastConformer and Mimi codes for audio. Finally the scores: word error rate, VoiceBench, MMLU, IFEval and GSM8K. Come back here whenever a name in the tables is unfamiliar.

MiniMind-O asks whether a complete omni model, one that listens, sees, reads and talks back, can work and stay fully open at only about 0.1 billion active parameters. The answer is yes: frozen SenseVoice and SigLIP2 encoders feed small projectors into the MiniMind language model, called the Thinker, and a separate four-layer Talker reads a middle Thinker layer and predicts eight Mimi codec streams that become streaming speech. The paper also shows which choices matter at this scale: the bridge layer, the Talker width, and low-rank codebook adapters. The tab runs from big picture and problem through method, equations and figures to results and a box on putting it into practice. Among the eleven papers it opens the omni group, after LFM2 and before Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3-Omni, MiniCPM-o 4.5 and Gemma 4, and it is the smallest model here that takes text, images and voice natively.

Every modality has its own entry path, and all of them end in the same 768-dimensional Thinker. Read each row left to right: raw input, encoder, projector, placeholder tokens. Dashed boxes are frozen, rust boxes are trainable projectors, and pink layer three is the bridge to the gold Talker. Notice that the voice to imitate enters only the Talker side, and that video is crossed out. This is the map of what the model takes in.

The usual cascade chains speech recognition, a language model and text-to-speech, so the language model never touches sound and errors cannot be traced to one shared representation. The lower row is MiniMind-O's alternative: encoders and projectors feed the Thinker, and a bridge passes its hidden state to a Talker that produces audio codes. The spoken output is then judged against the Thinker's own text, which is the evaluation idea behind Table 2 and Table 4.

Choosing which Thinker layer feeds the Talker is a trade-off between too little context and too much text bias. Layer zero still holds token identity, so it cannot decide how an ambiguous Chinese character is pronounced. Layer seven is bent toward picking the next text token, and the author saw Talker errors rise when the bridge moved deeper. The middle, layer three, is the default, given by equation u2 and used in Figure 2.

Eight parallel codebooks would multiply every audio embedding table and output head by eight. The grey bar is that full-rank cost, about 26 million parameters, which is computed here from the table sizes rather than stated in the paper. The gold part is the one shared base, and the rust part is the low-rank adapters, 11.8 million at rank 256 and 0.7 million at rank 16. Figure 8 later tests how small the rank can go.

The method is a pipeline of seven moves: encode, project, inject, think, bridge, speak and stream. Perception is delegated to frozen encoders, and only a thin MLP translates their frames into MiniMind's space, where they simply overwrite placeholder tokens. The Thinker then writes text, while the Talker reads a middle layer plus its own audio history and emits staggered codes that Mimi turns into sound. For fine-tuning, steps two, four and five are where trainable weights live.

Speech and images enter the Thinker by replacing placeholder embeddings, not through new attention layers. Blue cells are text tokens, gold cells are audio pad placeholders, one per speech frame, and teal cells are image pad placeholders, sixty-four per image. The arrows show projected SenseVoice frames and SigLIP2 tokens overwriting them. This is why the same sequence can mix any of the five input combinations in Figure 3, including spoken questions about an image.

Speech can start playing long before the text is finished because the eight codebooks are staggered. Each row is one Mimi codebook layer, gold cells are target codes and black cells are stop tokens. Layer q starts one step after layer q minus one, so after eight steps a complete frame exists, marked in pink, and the decoder can emit audio. Equation u6 writes this schedule down, and Figure 9 shows the resulting latency.

The whole training recipe is one script with three modes: all updates Thinker, Talker and projectors, while audio proj and vision proj train only one projector. The passes cover text-to-speech, audio projector alignment, three epochs of speech-to-speech, and image alignment and tuning, with small learning rates for full passes and larger ones for projector-only passes. No pass takes more than about seventy-five minutes on four RTX 3090 cards.

Equation one is the single training objective. L is the total loss, L text is the cross-entropy on the Thinker's response tokens, and the sum adds the eight audio losses, one per Mimi codebook layer q, weighted by lambda audio. Padding, reference codes and the speaker slot are masked, so only real targets count. The paper does not report the value of lambda, so treat it as a setting to find in the code.

The paper implies these standard forms rather than printing them.
