label: Fig. 4
text: Training happens in three stages that switch different parts on and off. Rust means trained and dashed means frozen. Stage one teaches Thinker and Talker to speak from text; stage two freezes both and aligns only the vision or audio projector; stage three tunes everything except the encoders and decoder on mixed text, audio and image instructions. Stage two is a ready-made template for a cheap, projector-only baseline in your own project.

label: Fig. 5
text: The actual token layout shows how a real prompt is written. The Thinker stream is a normal chat template: system, then user text, N audio pad tokens, a separator and sixty-four image pad tokens, then the assistant reply with an optional thinking trace. The Talker stream holds padding, a speaker slot, reference codes, then target codes and a stop. If you build your own dataset, it has to follow this layout.

label: Fig. 6
text: Text-to-speech training converges smoothly for both variants. Each panel plots a loss against training progress: total in black, text in indigo, audio in gold; solid is the dense 115 million model and dashed is the mixture-of-experts model with the same active size. Audio loss falls from about 6.5 to about 4, text loss from about 3.2 to about 1.35. The curves are redrawn in shape, and a spike from a bad checkpoint resume was removed by the author.

label: Fig. 7
text: Speech-to-speech training starts lower and stays noisier. Same layout as Figure 6: total, text and audio loss, dense solid and mixture-of-experts dashed. The mixture-of-experts model ends with slightly lower text loss and the dense model with slightly lower audio loss. The author reads this as a difference in how capacity is allocated, not as proof that one is better at equal compute. Shapes are redrawn.

label: Fig. 8
text: Moderate adapter ranks recover most of the benefit, and the output head matters more than the input embedding. Panels a to c sweep one shared rank: loss falls from rank 4 to rank 768, but the gain flattens after a few million parameters. Panels d to f decouple them: raising the head rank from 16 to 256 cuts final loss from 5.45 to 5.10, raising only the embedding rank reaches 5.35. It supports the low-rank design and hints where your own LoRA rank matters.

label: Fig. 9
text: Streaming makes the model feel fast even though the answer is long. The top timeline shows first text after about 140 milliseconds and first audio after about 260, while the text finishes at 9.6 seconds and the audio at 10.2. The lower timeline shows barge-in: when the voice activity detector hears the user again, the model aborts, listens, and starts a new reply. The author stresses this is a simple threshold, and the timings come from one example.

label: Fig. 10
text: Short spoken questions usually get sensible spoken answers, but English is weaker. Each card shows a spoken question, the text reply, and the length of the speech with its Mimi frame count. The four Chinese prompts get coherent answers; the two English ones here drift off-topic. That matches the training data, which is about seventy percent Chinese for speech-to-speech, and it gives you a ready fairness comparison for your evaluation.

label: Fig. 11
text: The image path works end to end, but it is the weakest part of the model. Each card shows an image, the gist of the spoken description, and our verdict. Three of eight are right, two are partly right, and three swap the main object, for example a rabbit described as a white fox. The author blames sixty-four image tokens and the tiny scale. For your task, keep the visual question narrow.

The released training data is large for such a small model. The text-to-speech set has about 1.25 million items with 1,636 hours of output speech; the speech-to-speech set has about 414 thousand items with 1,712 hours of input and 423 hours of output; the image set has about one hundred thousand items. Releasing it in the exact sequence format of Figure 5 is one of the paper's contributions, and it can seed your own dataset.

The Talker cannot be made thin. Rows vary the Talker hidden size for dense and mixture-of-experts models; the key column is average CER, lower is better. At 768 dimensions both variants reach about 0.09, while 512 and 384 dimensions raise the error up to about three times for a saving of about 19 to 27 million parameters. This is why 768 is kept, and it shows up in the chart just below.

Two trade-offs sit side by side here. On the left, bars show average CER for each Talker width, dense in indigo and mixture-of-experts in magenta: only 768 dimensions keeps the error near 0.09. On the right, voice similarity for the old reference-code-only baseline in grey against the two models: adding the speaker vector helps on both seen and unseen voices, though unseen voices stay lower. These are Tables 2 and 3 in picture form.

Adding the CAM++ speaker vector improves voice cloning. Numbers are cosine similarities between speaker embeddings of the reference and the generated speech, higher is better. Dense rises from 0.615 to 0.647 on seen voices, and mixture-of-experts reaches 0.570 on unseen voices against 0.531 for the baseline. The overall scores, about 0.60 and 0.59, are close; seen versus unseen voices is a natural fairness split.

Against two larger models, MiniMind-O is less consistent in English. The half-billion parameter Mini-Omni reaches a CER of about 0.01 and Mini-Omni2 about 0.037, while the 0.1 billion minimind-3o sits near 0.096. Table 8 and Table 9 show where that gap comes from: mid-length answers and a couple of number and name mismatches. Remember the model is about five times smaller.

The vision-language comparison uses nine synthetic images and references written by Qwen-VL-Plus. Both error rates are very high, around 0.76 to 0.82 CER, because many different descriptions of one image are all correct. MiniMind-O trails Mini-Omni2 but stays in the same range with one fifth of the parameters. The lesson for you: free-form captions are hard to score, so prefer short answers you can grade with accuracy.

This table is the parts list you need to understand the model and plan your GPU memory. The trainable Thinker has 63.9 million parameters in the dense version, the Talker 47 million, and the two projectors about one million each. The frozen SenseVoice encoder has 234 million, SigLIP2 about 95 million and the Mimi codec about 96 million. In total it is roughly half a billion parameters, which is small enough for a free T4.

Voice cloning depends more on the speaker than on the model variant. Bars show similarity per voice, indigo for dense and magenta for mixture-of-experts, seen voices on the left and held-out voices on the right. The best voices pass 0.70, while eric under mixture-of-experts and moon under dense fall to about 0.42 or 0.43. The author links low scores to degraded generated audio. It is a good template for a per-group fairness chart.

The per-speaker numbers behind the chart above. Each row is one voice with its cosine similarity for the dense and the mixture-of-experts model; the higher of the two is highlighted. The seen voices are the five shipped with the release, and the seven unseen ones were never used in training. The spread across voices, from about 0.40 to 0.73, is much larger than the gap between variants.

The English gap is concentrated in mid-length answers. Each cell gives CER, WER and the number of samples. On short answers of up to fifteen words, minimind-3o is close to Mini-Omni2, around 0.05 CER. On answers of sixteen to thirty words it jumps to about 0.13, while the larger models stay below 0.01. Sustaining pronunciation across a whole clause is the weak point, so keep your target answers short.

Most questions are perfect, and the few failures are mostly formatting. Each cell is CER and WER per question. Fourteen of twenty are zero for all three models. minimind-3o's worst case, question four, is the speed of light, where the number spoken correctly was transcribed in words, giving a CER of 1.41; question thirteen is a name variant. This is a clean example of why text normalization before scoring matters in any evaluation.

The per-image scores behind Table 5. Each cell gives the output length, the reference length, CER and WER for one of the nine images. MiniMind-O writes descriptions of similar length every time, about 109 to 137, while Mini-Omni2 varies more; its errors stay between about 0.76 and 0.87 CER. No single image breaks the model, but none is scored well either, which confirms how noisy this metric is.

Use this box as your plan. MiniMind-O already accepts text, voice and images, so you can skip the extra speech model and use its audio plus image format for spoken questions about pictures. The dense model should fit a free T4; add LoRA to the Thinker's attention and feed-forward layers, train the projectors, and keep the encoders frozen. Check fp16 and the missing LoRA mode in the repo first, then compare Chinese and English speakers and normalize numbers before scoring.

label: Primer
text: Speech travels two different roads in MiniMind-O. On the way in, the sixteen kilohertz waveform becomes a log-mel spectrogram, the frozen SenseVoice encoder turns it into feature frames, and a small trainable projector drops each frame into an audio pad slot of the language model. On the way out, the Talker predicts Mimi codes, eight for every eighty millisecond frame, and the frozen Mimi decoder rebuilds twenty four kilohertz audio. On the input side, only the rust projector learns.

label: Primer
text: An image enters the model as sixty four extra tokens. SigLIP2 cuts a two hundred fifty six pixel square into an eight by eight grid of patches and outputs one vector per patch. The trainable projector translates those vectors into MiniMind's space, where they replace sixty four image pad placeholders between ordinary text tokens, as the strip at the bottom shows. For your own project, training only this projector is the cheapest way to adapt the vision side.

label: Primer
text: MiniMind-O splits thinking from speaking. The eight layer Thinker writes the text answer, while its layer three hidden state, shown in pink, feeds a four block Talker that predicts the audio codes. Each of the eight codebook rows starts one step later than the row above, so the codes form a staircase. Once the first full column exists, the decoder can play sound, which is why speech starts long before the text is finished.

label: Primer
text: Here is MiniMind-O's place in the atlas. LFM2, the tab before, gave a fast small backbone with vision and audio in separate variants. MiniMind-O is the first model in our order that hears, sees and speaks in one small, fully open package, trainable on four consumer GPUs in under four hours per cycle. Qwen2.5-Omni, the next tab, uses the same Thinker and Talker design at seven billion parameters and adds video.

These fourteen terms are the vocabulary of this paper. Three matter most. The Thinker is the language model that writes text, and the Talker turns its hidden states into speech. Mimi codes are the discrete audio tokens the Talker predicts, eight per frame. CER, the character error rate, measures how well the spoken answer matches the text answer after transcription, and you can reuse it as a metric in your own evaluation.

Qwen2.5-Omni asks whether one open model can read text, images, audio and video together and answer both in writing and in natural speech, in real time. Its answer is a 7 billion parameter model split into a Thinker, the language model that understands and writes, and a Talker that turns the Thinker's hidden states into streaming speech, with a position scheme called TMRoPE that puts video frames and sound on one clock. The tab starts with the big picture of every input path, then the three problems, the method and training stages, every equation, the four figures redrawn, all ten result tables with three charts, and a box on putting the model into practice. Among the eleven papers it is the second omni model, after MiniMind-O and before Qwen3-Omni, and the one where voice input is fully native.

label: Overview
text: Each input type has its own lane: text goes through the tokenizer, images and video through one shared vision transformer, and voice through an audio encoder, all ending as tokens for the same Thinker. Indigo marks text and the language model, teal vision, gold audio and speech, magenta the paper's key mechanisms. Notice that voice is a native input, so you need no separate speech recognizer, while image or video generation is not supported.

label: Problem
text: Three problems motivate the whole design. On the left, plain one dimensional positions place a video frame and the audio from the same second far apart, so the model cannot tell they belong together. In the middle, one decoder trained to emit both text and speech mixes two training signals. On the right are the four sources of delay before the user hears anything, listed without numbers. TMRoPE, the Thinker-Talker split and the streaming designs answer these in turn.

This list answers the first practical question: how each modality becomes tokens. Text uses byte-level BPE with about 151 thousand tokens. Audio becomes a 128 channel mel spectrogram and then roughly one token per 40 milliseconds. Images pass through a 675 million parameter vision transformer whose neighbouring patches are merged two by two. Video reuses the same encoder at a dynamic frame rate. TMRoPE then gives everything positions on a shared clock,, and the last two steps produce output.

label: Talker
text: The Talker gets two inputs because each one covers the other's weakness. The Thinker's hidden state, in magenta, carries meaning, tone and attitude before the sentence is finished, which lets speech start early and sound natural. But hidden states group words by meaning, not by sound, so two different-sounding words can look alike; the sampled text tokens, in indigo, remove that doubt. The paper also stresses that no word or timestamp alignment between text and speech is needed for training.

label: Training
text: Read this left to right as a timeline, with rust meaning trained in that stage and grey meaning frozen. Stage one locks the language model and trains the adapters and then the encoders. Stage two unfreezes everything and adds about 800 billion image and video tokens, 300 billion audio tokens and 100 billion video-with-audio tokens. Stage three extends context to 32,768 tokens. The Talker then gets its own three stages, with the magenta DPO step described by equation one.

This is the paper's example of instruction data in ChatML format, a template you can copy for fine-tuning. Each turn opens with an im start tag and a role, video content sits between vision start and vision end tags, and the assistant's answer ends with im end. Notice that the second user turn has no typed question at all: the question is spoken inside the video, so the model must listen. It is transcribed as printed.

The paper names four delays that add up before a user hears the first sound, and this list pairs each with its fix. Input encoding is made streamable by running audio attention in two second blocks and making the vision encoder efficient. The Talker can start speaking from hidden states while text is still being written. The code-to-wave decoder only looks at a few neighbouring blocks, so audio starts early. The fourth factor, model size, is named but not quantified.

This is the direct preference optimisation loss of the Talker's second stage, the paper's only numbered equation. For input text x, y w is a good speech sample and y l a bad one. The loss rewards the Talker, P theta, for raising the likelihood of the good sample relative to a frozen reference model P ref, more than the bad one; beta sets strength, sigma is the sigmoid. Good and bad are ranked by word error rate and punctuation pause errors.

label: (text)
text: This is not a paper equation but the TMRoPE rules from section 2.2 written out. Every token gets three position numbers: temporal, height and width. For text and audio all three are equal, which makes it behave like ordinary one dimensional RoPE. For audio the number is absolute time tau divided into 40 millisecond steps, k, so 25 steps make one second. This is what lets sound and video share one clock in figure three.

label: (text)
text: Also written out from the paper's text, not a numbered equation. A visual token in row i and column j of frame f gets height i, width j, and a temporal ID taken from the frame's real timestamp tau f in 40 millisecond steps. Because the ID follows real time, a variable frame rate does not break alignment with audio. When modalities follow each other, the next one starts one past the largest ID used so far.

label: (text)
text: This mask, derived from figure four and not printed in the paper, says which code blocks the speech decoder may attend to. M i j is one when block j lies between two blocks before block i and one block after it, and zero otherwise. So each block sees four blocks in total. The small lookahead is why the decoder can start producing audio before the Talker has finished all its codes.

label: (text)
text: A token budget implied by section 2.2, not a paper equation. Audio sampled at 16 kilohertz with a 10 millisecond hop gives 100 mel frames per second, and the encoder outputs about one token per 40 milliseconds, so roughly 25 audio tokens per second. A ten second voice clip therefore costs about 250 tokens. For free Colab experiments this is the number that tells you how much memory voice input will take.

label: Fig. 1
text: The teaser shows the promise: one model handles video chat, text chat, image chat and audio chat, and can always answer out loud. In the centre, See and Hear are the vision and audio encoders, feeding the Thinker, then the Talker and a streaming codec decoder. The four panels are paraphrased examples, such as solving a small algebra problem from an image or describing a piece of music. It is a map of capabilities, not a result.

label: Fig. 2
text: This is the architecture in one picture. At the bottom, video frames and the sound track run along time into the vision and audio encoders. The Thinker reads a text prompt, then interleaved vision and audio tokens, then samples its own text answer, shown by the dashed loop. Above it, the Talker reads the Thinker's hidden states, the sampled text tokens and its own codec track, and emits codec tokens to the streaming decoder. The layout is simplified.

label: Fig. 3
text: Each video frame's tokens share a temporal ID and get height and width IDs from their place in the grid; audio tokens get three equal IDs that move one step every 40 milliseconds. Frames one second apart get temporal IDs 0, 25, 50 and so on, lining up with the audio IDs. Each two second chunk is fed as vision first, then its audio. A repeated label in the original is corrected here.

label: Fig. 4
text: Rows are query blocks of speech codes and columns are key blocks; a coloured cell means attention is allowed. Magenta is the current block, pink and grey the two past blocks, gold the single future block, and white is masked. This limited window, used in the flow-matching DiT, lets the model emit audio chunk by chunk instead of waiting for the whole utterance. It is the fix for the third latency source in the problem panel.

label: Chart
text: On OmniBench, which asks questions combining images, audio and text, Qwen2.5-Omni reaches an average of 56.13 percent, while the best other system, Gemini 1.5 Pro, reaches 42.91 percent and the other open omni models stay below 43. This is the paper's strongest evidence that feeding all modalities into one Thinker with shared positions helps joint understanding, not just single-modality tasks. The full breakdown by speech, sound and music is in table eight.

label: Chart
text: Lower bars are better here: this is word error rate when speech generated by each system is transcribed, on the hard SEED test set. The DPO stage cuts Qwen2.5-Omni's error from 7.97 to 6.54, close to Seed-TTS after reinforcement learning at 6.42 and better than CosyVoice 2 at 6.83. It shows that equation one, preference training on good and bad speech, mainly buys stability on difficult sentences.

label: Chart
text: The gold bars are Qwen2.5-Omni answering spoken questions, the indigo bars a text model answering the same questions typed, and the grey bars the older Qwen2-Audio. Gold sits close to indigo and far above grey, and on GSM8K it is even higher, 85.4 against 82.3. The gap is still large on CEval and IFEval. This comparison, spoken versus typed input, is a ready-made experiment design for your own project.

Table one checks the price of adding modalities: plain text ability. Qwen2.5-Omni generally lands between Qwen2-7B and Qwen2.5-7B, its own starting point. For example it scores 71.5 on MATH against 75.5 for Qwen2.5-7B, and 47.0 on MMLU-Pro against 56.3. So the omni training costs some text skill but keeps most of it, a fair trade the paper reports honestly.

Table two lists speech recognition word error rates, where lower is better, and speech translation BLEU scores, where higher is better. Qwen2.5-Omni is competitive everywhere and best on several sets, for example 5.2 on Common Voice Chinese and 3.0 on Fleurs Chinese. Notice the spread across languages: Cantonese at 7.3 is worse than Qwen2-Audio's 5.9. That uneven quality across languages is exactly the kind of fairness question worth testing in your own project.

Table three covers audio understanding beyond words: emotion in speech, vocal sounds, music, audio reasoning and voice chatting. Qwen2.5-Omni leads on emotion recognition at 0.570 and on the MMAU reasoning benchmark with an average of 65.60, far above Gemini Pro 1.5 at 54.90. On VoiceBench its overall average of 74.12 is the best among the listed models. The audio encoder clearly hears more than transcripts.

Table four is the source of the spoken versus typed chart. Questions from text benchmarks were turned into speech, about 90 percent of them, and given to Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen2-Audio, while Qwen2-7B got the typed text. Qwen2.5-Omni closes most of the gap, for instance 65.6 against 69.3 on MMLU, compared with 33.2 for Qwen2-Audio. It supports the paper's claim that voice commands work nearly as well as text.

Table five compares image understanding with Qwen2.5-VL-7B, the vision-only model whose encoder Qwen2.5-Omni reuses, plus GPT-4o-mini and the best other omni model. The omni model stays within about a point of Qwen2.5-VL on most rows, such as 95.2 against 95.7 on DocVQA, and wins a few, like MME-RealWorld. Adding audio and speech therefore costs very little vision quality.

Table six tests visual grounding, meaning finding the box or point that matches a phrase. Qwen2.5-Omni matches or beats Qwen2.5-VL on most RefCOCO splits, for example 93.5 on RefCOCO test A, and reaches 42.2 mAP on open-vocabulary detection, though the specialist Grounding DINO is still better there at 55.0. It shows the vision lane keeps fine spatial detail.

Table seven covers video without its sound, plus Video-MME with subtitles. Qwen2.5-Omni is best on three of four rows, for example 72.4 on Video-MME with subtitles and 68.6 on EgoSchema, and just below Qwen2.5-VL without subtitles. Together with the TMRoPE figure, it shows the time-aware positions do not hurt pure video understanding.

Table eight is the full OmniBench result behind the bar chart, split into questions whose audio is speech, sound events or music. Qwen2.5-Omni leads on speech at 55.25 percent and sound events at 60.00 percent, while video-SALMONN is better on music. The average of 56.13 percent is well ahead of every other system, supporting the paper's claim of state of the art multimodal understanding.

Table nine evaluates the Talker as a zero-shot text to speech system on SEED, with word error rate, lower is better, and speaker similarity, higher is better. The in-context-learning version is decent; after the DPO stage the error drops to 1.42, 2.33 and 6.54 on the three test sets. Speaker similarity stays a little below Seed-TTS. The key reading is the jump from ICL to RL rows.

Table ten shows what speaker fine-tuning adds. Four fine-tuned voices, A to D, keep error rates close to human recordings, and some beat the base RL model, such as 1.83 on the English test for speaker D. Naturalness scores reach 4.51 in Chinese and 4.62 in English for speaker B, equal to or above the human reference of 4.51 in Chinese. This is the Talker's third training stage paying off.

Use this box as a checklist before you start the notebook. Since voice is native, you can skip an extra speech recognizer, but running Whisper as a baseline makes a good comparison. Check memory first: load the smallest checkpoint in four bit, turn off speech output, keep clips short, and put LoRA only on the Thinker's attention and MLP layers. Then build ChatML samples like the paper's example and plan the typed versus spoken and per-language tests.

label: Primer
text: Before a language model can reason about a photo or a voice note, both must become tokens. The teal lane cuts an image into fourteen pixel patches, runs them through a vision transformer and merges each two by two group into one token. The gold lane turns a recording into a log-mel spectrogram, and a Whisper based encoder emits about twenty five tokens per second. Longer clips and bigger images cost more GPU memory.

label: Primer
text: Speaking works like writing, only with a different vocabulary. The Talker predicts speech codec tokens from the Thinker's hidden states; a flow matching DiT turns those codes into a mel spectrogram, and BigVGAN turns that into sound. The timeline below shows why streaming matters: making audio in chunks lets the first sound play early. For a text answer task you can skip the Talker entirely and fine-tune only for text answers.

label: Primer
text: Every token needs a position, and plain counting treats a video as frames first, then sound, so a frame and its own audio end up far apart. TMRoPE replaces the count with a clock: one time step equals forty milliseconds, so a frame at one second and the audio at one second both get time ID twenty five. Image patches also get height and width IDs. This is the paper's main new idea for video with sound.

label: Primer
text: This is paper eight of eleven. MiniMind-O, just before, is a tiny omni model you can read line by line; Qwen2.5-Omni is the full scale version at seven billion parameters, with native text, image, video and voice input and streaming speech output. Qwen3-Omni, the larger model after it, keeps the same Thinker and Talker split. Because text, image and voice inputs are all native, you need no extra speech to text model.

These fourteen terms are the vocabulary the paper takes for granted. The most important are the Thinker and Talker, the two halves of the model; TMRoPE, its time aligned position scheme; and speech codec tokens, which let a model speak one token at a time. Keep WER in mind too: you will likely report it for voice experiments, and you should normalise transcripts before computing it.

Can one model hear, see and read at once without getting worse at any of them? Qwen3-Omni says yes, and it is a larger reference model, read for ideas rather than fine-tuned on a small GPU. A thirty billion parameter mixture-of-experts Thinker, with three billion active per token, reads text, images, audio and video. A smaller Talker turns the Thinker's hidden states into streaming speech. The tab starts with the big picture of every input path. It then covers the problems the paper fixes, the method with its audio encoder, time-aligned positions, streaming speech and training recipe, the relations the paper states in prose, all its figures, all eighteen tables, and a box on putting it into practice. In the atlas it is the ninth of eleven papers: after QLoRA, TinyLLaVA Factory, SmolVLM, Voxtral, Voxtral Realtime, LFM2, MiniMind-O and Qwen2.5-Omni, and before MiniCPM-o 4.5 and Gemma 4.

Every input has its own path into one language model; read each row left to right. Text in indigo goes straight to tokens, images and video in teal share the vision encoder, and audio in gold becomes AuT tokens at twelve and a half per second. The magenta TM-RoPE column gives all tokens a shared time axis before the Thinker reads them. The bottom row is the speech output path; images and video are never generated.

Adding modalities to a language model usually costs something somewhere. The left panel shows the typical pattern, with the text bar falling below the dashed line of a same-size single-modality model. The right panel shows the paper's claim that every modality reaches that line. The heights are illustrative only. The real evidence is the controlled comparison in Table sixteen and its delta chart in the results.

Speech output used to wait for a whole block of tokens. In the upper row, Qwen two point five Omni's Talker collects a block before a diffusion vocoder can render audio. In the lower row, Qwen3-Omni needs one Talker token, one MTP step and one small ConvNet pass, and then the first sound plays. Only the two hundred thirty-four millisecond figure comes from the paper; the lengths are schematic. The streaming Talker diagram later shows how this works.

Voice becomes about twelve and a half tokens per second. The top strip is the raw sixteen kilohertz waveform. Below it, one mel frame is computed every ten milliseconds. Three convolution blocks merge every eight frames into one token covering eighty milliseconds, which is what the dashed lines group. This is why forty minutes of audio fits into about thirty thousand tokens, and it tells you how long your own voice clips will be in tokens.

TM-RoPE decides where each token sits in time and space. The top bar is the older M-RoPE, which gives time only the first sixteen rotary angles, the fastest-spinning ones. The middle bar interleaves time, height and width across twenty-four, twenty and twenty angles. The bottom strip is a toy example of position ids: text uses one shared number, an image patch keeps one time id plus its row and column, and audio advances one step every eighty milliseconds.

These six steps follow one request from raw input to answer. Text is tokenized, images and video pass through the shared vision encoder, and voice passes through the mel front end and AuT. TM-RoPE then puts everything on one time axis so the Thinker can read a single sequence. Speaking is an optional last step for the Talker. This list is also the skeleton of a one-page explanation of the inputs.

The Talker speaks one eighty millisecond frame at a time. Read each column from the bottom up. The Talker predicts codebook zero, the magenta MTP module fills in residual codebooks one to fifteen, their embeddings are summed, and Code2Wav turns the sum into audio. The dashed arrows show that the summed frame becomes the next Talker input. Because the ConvNet only looks at past frames, sound can start after the very first frame.

This loop is our sketch of sections two point four and two point five, not an algorithm box from the paper. The Talker is conditioned once on the Thinker's context, then loops over frames. In each pass it samples codebook zero, lets the small MTP module add the residual codes, sums their embeddings, and hands them to Code2Wav, which emits eighty milliseconds of audio right away. The same logic appears as equation five and in the streaming Talker diagram.

Table one is the parts list. The Thinker is the thirty billion parameter mixture of experts with three billion active. Around it sit the six hundred fifty million parameter AuT audio encoder, the five hundred forty million parameter SigLIP two vision encoder, the three billion parameter Talker, the eighty million parameter MTP module and the two hundred million parameter Code2Wav. Notice that the whole system is far larger than three billion, which matters for memory.

Table two breaks first-packet latency into sequential stages at one, four and six simultaneous streams, with audio and video values separated by a slash. With one stream, audio reaches two hundred thirty-four milliseconds and video five hundred forty-seven. The Thinker's time to first token grows fastest with load, while MTP and codec stay at a few milliseconds. The real-time factor stays below one, so speech is always produced faster than it plays. These are theoretical numbers on vLLM.

Table three lists language coverage, which differs sharply by modality. Text covers one hundred nineteen languages. Speech input covers nineteen, including Arabic, Urdu and Cantonese. Speech output covers only ten, and Arabic is not among them. If your fairness experiment compares Arabic and English, this table tells you the model can hear Arabic but cannot answer in Arabic speech.

Rust marks what is trained in each stage, grey what is frozen. In the first pre-training stage the Qwen3 language model is frozen while each encoder's adapter is trained first and the encoder second. Stages two and three train everything, first on about two trillion mixed tokens, then with a longer context. The two lower lanes show separate post-training for the Thinker and for the Talker. The frozen-backbone, adapter-first pattern in stage one resembles the LoRA setups you will build.

The training recipe runs in three phases. Pre-training aligns the encoders to a frozen language model, then trains everything on mixed data, then stretches the context. The Thinker is post-trained with supervised fine-tuning, distillation from larger Qwen3 teachers and reinforcement learning with rule-based and judge-based rewards. The Talker gets its own four stages ending in speaker fine-tuning. The Captioner shows that the released model can be fine-tuned further for a new task.

label: (i)
text: Relation one computes the audio token rate. One divided by eight times ten milliseconds gives twelve and a half tokens per second, so each token covers eighty milliseconds. Multiply forty minutes by sixty seconds by twelve and a half and you get about thirty thousand tokens, our own arithmetic. Use the same calculation to estimate sequence lengths for your voice clips before you fine-tune.

label: (ii)
text: Relation two is the TM-RoPE budget. Sixty-four rotary angles are shared as twenty-four for time t, twenty for height h and twenty for width w, and they are interleaved rather than stacked in blocks. Under M-RoPE, time used only angles one to sixteen. Spreading time across fast and slow frequencies is what the paper credits for better handling of long audio and video.

label: (iii)
text: Relation three gives the position ids for each modality. For text, t, h and w all equal the token index n, which reduces to ordinary one-dimensional RoPE. For an image, time is a fixed start value s, and height and width add the patch row r and column c. For audio and video, time is s plus the real timestamp tau divided by eighty milliseconds. The image offset is our reading of M-RoPE, so treat it as approximate.

label: (iv)
text: Relation four keeps positions from colliding. The start offset of the next modality, s sub m plus one, is one more than the largest position id used by the previous modality m. This is the dashed arrow in the TM-RoPE diagram.

label: (v)
text: Relation five, in our notation, describes one speech frame. The frame embedding e sub k is the sum over codebooks j from zero to J of each codebook's embedding table E sub j applied to its chosen code c. The zeroth code is sampled from a softmax over a linear head on the Talker state h sub k. The MTP module predicts the remaining J codes, fifteen in Figure two, and the sum feeds Code2Wav and the next Talker step.

label: (vi)
text: Relation six says first-packet latency is simply a sum, because the stages run one after another: pre-processing, the Thinker's time to first token, the Talker's time to first token, one MTP step and one codec step. With one audio stream that is seventy-two plus eighty-eight plus fifty-seven plus fourteen plus three, which equals two hundred thirty-four milliseconds. The same check for video gives five hundred forty-seven.

label: (vii)
text: Relation seven is the real-time factor: the time to produce one frame, Thinker token plus Talker token plus MTP plus codec, divided by the eighty milliseconds that frame lasts. Below one means speech is generated faster than it plays. With Table two's single-stream rates, about thirteen plus seven plus fourteen plus three milliseconds gives about thirty-seven and a half, a factor of about zero point four seven, matching the paper. The check is ours.

label: (viii)
text: Relation eight is on-policy distillation. The student samples its own answer y, and at each step t its next-token distribution p theta is pulled toward the teacher's by minimising the KL divergence. The teacher is Qwen3 thirty-two B or the two hundred thirty-five billion parameter model. The paper does not state the direction of the KL, so the order shown is an assumption. This is the second stage of Thinker post-training.

label: Fig. 1
text: Figure one is the teaser, arranged as four promises. Smarter shows thinking mode solving an integral. Multilingual shows a spoken question answered by transcribing French. Faster quotes the two hundred thirty-four millisecond first packet. Longer shows a thirty-minute meeting transcript. It carries no data. It previews the claims that Tables five, six and two later back with numbers.

label: Fig. 2
text: Figure two is the whole architecture on one page. At the bottom, frames pass the teal vision encoder and the soundtrack gold AuT, and their hidden states sit between indigo prompt tokens. The Thinker writes text, which loops back as input. Hidden states from its middle layers feed the gold Talker, which predicts codebook zero, and the magenta MTP stack adds codebooks one to fifteen before the streaming decoder renders sound.

label: Fig. 3
text: Figure three shows how AuT is built. It is trained as a full speech-to-text model: filter-bank features pass through three downsampling convolution blocks and thirty-two attention layers, and an eight-layer decoder writes the transcript. The decoder is used only during training on twenty million hours of audio. Qwen3-Omni keeps just the encoder, about six hundred million parameters, as its ear. This is the audio encoder box in the big picture.

label: App. 9.2
text: Appendix nine point two contains three long captions, not numbered figures, redrawn here as summary cards. The Captioner describes a comic Mandarin monologue, a cinematic sound-effect scene and a sci-fi clip mixing dialogue, machinery and music, noting timing, tone and setting. They are qualitative examples with no metric, so read them as a demonstration of fine-tuning the model for a new audio task, not as proof of accuracy.

Most bars sit within about one point of zero, which is what no degradation looks like. Each bar is the Omni base model's score minus a same-size base trained on only text, in indigo, or only vision, in teal, with matched data, schedule and compute. EvalPlus gains over four points. MVBench and RealWorldQA lose a little over two. This chart is the main evidence for the paper's headline claim.

Most of the wait is the Thinker thinking of its first token. Each stacked bar splits first-packet latency into pre-processing in grey, Thinker in indigo, Talker in gold, and the thin MTP and codec slices. At one stream audio takes two hundred thirty-four milliseconds, and at six streams video grows past two seconds. The video parts at six streams add up to three milliseconds more than the total the paper prints, a small inconsistency in the source.

Qwen3-Omni Instruct, the dark gold bar, has the lowest word error rate of these five systems on LibriSpeech other, WenetSpeech meeting and CommonVoice English. The caveat is the nineteen-language Fleurs average, where GPT four o Transcribe does better, four point four eight against five point three three. Lower bars are better. Note that the multilingual number is only an average, so it hides per-language gaps such as Arabic.

Turning on reasoning makes transcription worse. For each test set the gold bar is Instruct and the indigo bar is the Thinking model, and indigo is longer everywhere, most on sung lyrics, where Opencpop jumps from about one and a half to about six. The paper concludes that step-by-step reasoning does not help perception tasks and may add hallucinations. For your fine-tuning, a plain instruct model is the better starting point for speech recognition.

Table four compares instruct models on text. Qwen3-Omni Instruct stays close to the text-only Qwen3 thirty B Instruct and beats GPT four o and the larger non-thinking Qwen3 two hundred thirty-five B on reasoning sets like AIME twenty-five and ZebraLogic. The text-only model still wins most rows, for example ZebraLogic ninety against seventy-six. So text ability is largely kept, with some gaps at the instruct level.

Table five does the same for reasoning models. Qwen3-Omni Thinking is competitive but rarely the best. It wins on WritingBench, while Gemini two point five Flash Thinking and the text-only Qwen3 models lead on GPQA, AIME twenty-five and BFCL. Read it together with Table four: the omni model is roughly on par in text, not better.

Table six is the speech recognition and speech translation scoreboard, and the most relevant table for voice input. Word error rate is lower-better and BLEU is higher-better. Qwen3-Omni Instruct is best on most English and Chinese sets and on lyrics, but Gemini two point five Pro leads translation and GPT four o Transcribe leads the nineteen-language average. The footnotes matter for your normalization experiment: lyric transcripts are converted to Simplified Chinese before scoring.

Table seven tests spoken instructions and audio reasoning. VoiceBench asks questions by voice. Qwen3-Omni Thinking and Flash Thinking score about eighty-nine overall, just behind Gemini two point five Pro at eighty-nine point six. On audio reasoning, the Instruct models lead MMAU. Here, unlike transcription, the Thinking model helps, because the tasks need reasoning after listening.

Table eight covers music understanding: genre, mood, instrument and tagging. Qwen3-Omni Instruct beats both the best specialist models and the general audio models on every row, for example ninety-three percent on GTZAN genre accuracy. The metric is micro F1 for the tagging sets, because language models output label sets without probabilities.

Table nine checks image and video understanding for instruct models. Qwen3-Omni Instruct is close to the much larger Qwen two point five VL seventy-two B, and it leads on math-heavy sets such as MathVista and MATH-Vision. Document and chart questions are slightly behind the seventy-two B model. Long-video results are mixed, which the paper blames on limited positional extrapolation and context length.

Table ten repeats the vision comparison for reasoning models. The Qwen3-Omni Thinking models lead on HallusionBench, MM-MT-Bench, ChartQA and CountBench. Gemini and InternVL three point five lead on MMMU, MathVista and long video. The takeaway matches Table nine: strong image reasoning, weaker long-video understanding.

Table eleven has a single benchmark, WorldSense, which needs sound and picture together. Qwen3-Omni Instruct scores fifty-four, ahead of Gemini two point five Flash at about fifty-one and Qwen two point five Omni at about forty-five. It is the paper's main evidence for joint audio-visual understanding at the instruct level.

Table twelve tests audio-visual reasoning with the Thinking models. On DailyOmni and VideoHolmes, Qwen3-Omni Thinking beats the previous open-source best and Gemini two point five Flash Thinking. Together with Table eleven it supports the claim that the model reasons across sound and video, not just within each.

Table thirteen measures text-to-speech quality as word error rate: the generated speech is transcribed and compared with the input text. Qwen3-Omni has the best English score at one point three nine. CosyVoice three is best in Chinese. Lower is better, and the paper credits reinforcement learning for the stability of its English speech.

Table fourteen checks voice cloning in ten languages. The first three columns are word error rate, lower is better; the last three are speaker similarity, higher is better. Qwen3-Omni has the lowest error in half the languages, including Chinese, English and French, while ElevenLabs or MiniMax win the others, and similarity is close to MiniMax. The table is a reminder that quality varies by language even inside one model.

Table fifteen measures cross-lingual voice cloning: speaking in one language with a voice from another. Word error rate is lower-better. Qwen3-Omni wins every direction into English and Korean, while CosyVoice three leads all directions into Japanese and most into Chinese. The caption's note is useful for your normalization experiment: Qwen3-Omni is scored on Japanese without text normalization, while CosyVoice three converts Japanese to kana.

Table sixteen is the controlled experiment behind the no-degradation claim. Three base models of the same size, text-only, vision-only and omni, were trained on the same data per modality with matched compute. The omni model is best on most rows. The single-modality models win a few by small margins, such as MMLU-Pro and MultiPL-E for text, and RealWorldQA and MVBench for vision. The delta chart above shows the same numbers as differences.

Table seventeen, in the appendix, repeats the speech recognition table for the Thinking models. Compare it row by row with Table six: the Thinking model is worse almost everywhere, for example CommonVoice English rises from about six to about ten and a half. This is the data behind the Instruct versus Thinking chart and the paper's advice not to use reasoning for perception.

Table eighteen, in the appendix, repeats the music table for the Thinking models. Scores drop compared with Instruct in Table eight, for instance GTZAN falls from ninety-three to eighty-nine. It confirms the pattern from Table seventeen: reasoning mode does not help tasks that are mostly about perceiving sound.

Use this paper as a map, not as your model. It handles text, image and voice inputs natively, but every released variant is thirty billion parameters, too large for QLoRA on a free sixteen gigabyte T four, so pick a smaller model such as Qwen two point five Omni. Borrow the ideas instead: LoRA on attention with frozen encoders, a spoken-question-about-an-image task, and a fairness test on Arabic versus English, where this paper reports no per-language numbers.

label: Primer
text: Before a model can reason about a question, a photo and a voice clip, all three must become tokens. Text goes through a sub-word tokenizer, the image is cut into patches for a vision encoder, and audio becomes a mel spectrogram that the AuT encoder squeezes into one token every eighty milliseconds. TM-RoPE puts every token on one shared time axis, so the Thinker reads a single sequence. This is exactly what you should be able to explain first.

label: Primer
text: Thirty B A three B is the most important label on this model. A router inside each mixture-of-experts layer sends every token to only a few experts, so about three billion parameters do the work per token. But all thirty billion must be loaded, which is about fifteen gigabytes at four bits before anything else. That is why you read this paper for ideas and fine-tune a smaller model on the free T4.

label: Primer
text: To speak, the model does not produce a waveform directly. It predicts codec codes: for every eighty milliseconds of speech, the Talker picks code zero, the small MTP module fills in codes one to fifteen, and Code2Wav turns them into sound at once. Because no block of frames has to be collected first, the first sound can arrive after about two hundred thirty four milliseconds. The timeline is a sketch, not a measurement.

label: Primer
text: Qwen3-Omni is the ninth of eleven papers and a larger reference model, read for ideas rather than trained on a small GPU. It inherits the Thinker and Talker split from Qwen2.5-Omni in the previous tab, and adds mixture-of-experts for both halves, its own AuT audio encoder, time-aligned positions and codec-based streaming speech. It takes text, image and voice natively, plus video. MiniCPM-o 4.5 comes next.

Keep this glossary open while you read the tab. The terms you will meet most often are Thinker and Talker, mixture of experts, AuT, TM-RoPE and codebook. For your experiments, word error rate matters most: it counts wrong words in a transcript, and its value changes with how you normalize text, which is the point of a with and without normalization experiment. The benchmark names tell you which modality each table tests.

MiniCPM-o 4.5 asks how a small open model can see, listen and speak at the same time, instead of taking turns like a walkie-talkie. Its answer is a nine billion parameter model that turns images, video and audio into tokens for a Qwen3 eight B language model, and a framework called Omni-Flow that cuts the live stream into one-second chunks so the model reads new input and writes its reply in every chunk. The tab moves from the big picture of every input path, through the problem, the method, every equation and figure, to the result tables and a box on putting it into practice. In the atlas it is the tenth of eleven papers, in the omni group after MiniMind-O, Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni, and just before Gemma 4. For a text, image and voice project, it is a clean example where all three inputs are native.

Every input ends up as tokens for one language model, and this diagram shows each path from left to right. Teal is vision: an image is cut into slices, SigLIP makes 1024 tokens per slice, and a resampler squeezes them to 64. Gold is audio: Whisper makes 50 tokens per second and a small MLP merges them down to 10. Indigo is text and the Qwen3 backbone. This is the picture you need to explain how each input gets in.

Three separate problems motivate the paper. On the top left, a turn-based model stops perceiving while it speaks, so new input is ignored. Bottom left, if the language model had to write speech tokens itself it would need about 25 decode steps per second instead of three or four. On the right, speech that lags behind the text describes a scene that has already changed. Omni-Flow, the speech decoder and TAIL each fix one of these.

These five steps are the whole input story in compact form: how text, image, video and voice each enter the model and how speech comes out. The logic is the same for every modality. A pretrained encoder turns raw signal into features, a small projector compresses them into a few tokens the language model can read, and the language model does the reasoning. Speech output reverses the idea, with the model's hidden states steering a small speech decoder.

Omni-Flow is the paper's key mechanism, and it is simpler than it sounds. Each one-second chunk is written as visual tokens, then audio tokens, then whatever the model says in that second. If it has nothing to say, it writes a single listen token. Chaining the chunks gives one ordinary sequence, so a standard causal language model can be trained on it. Deciding whether to speak becomes just another next-token prediction.

Rust boxes are trained and grey boxes are frozen in each of the four training stages. In stage one only the new audio projector, the projector from the language model to speech, and the speech decoder learn, so vision and language skills are not disturbed. From stage two everything is unfrozen. This staged recipe is a useful model for your own fine-tuning: add adapters, keep the big pretrained parts frozen.

This procedure shows how the training data for time-aligned speech is built. For each one-second chunk, collect the text tokens that start being spoken in that second, attach their speech tokens, and push the speech of the last few tokens into the next chunk so pronunciation can see the next word. Because the amount of text per chunk varies, the model learns to write less when its voice is running behind.

g k equals the list of v k, a k and o k: the visual tokens, audio tokens and output tokens of chunk k. The full sequence is simply g one, g two, g three and so on, one after the other. This single line is how the paper turns a continuous live conversation into something a normal causal language model can read and train on, as drawn in the Omni-Flow diagram.

A text token j belongs to chunk k exactly when its start time falls between k minus one times t and k times t, where t is the chunk length of one second. This is the rule behind TAIL. It ties each word to the second in which it is actually spoken, so the model's text and its voice stay on the same clock.

These two token budgets explain why the model is cheap enough for streaming. Audio goes from 50 Whisper tokens per second to 10 after a five times merge by the MLP. Each image slice goes from 1024 SigLIP tokens to 64 after the resampler, a sixteen times compression where many models use four. Fewer tokens also means shorter sequences and less memory when you fine-tune.

Equation one is the length reward used in reinforcement learning. For each prompt, s i is 0.5 minus the response length rescaled between the shortest and longest answer, times a factor that shrinks when lengths barely differ, controlled by tau. Correct answers get s i, so short correct answers earn up to half a point. Wrong answers get the minimum of zero and s i, so being short never rescues a wrong answer.

label: Fig. 1
text: Each spoke is one benchmark, grouped into omni-modal, speech and vision arcs, and each axis is rescaled so the best model shown sits on the outer ring. The magenta MiniCPM-o line hugs the outside on the omni and speech axes and stays close to Gemini 2.5 Flash on vision. Compare positions, not areas, since the scaling is per axis. This is the paper's headline claim in one picture.

label: Fig. 2
text: Interaction with AI is drawn as four steps from left to right: text chat, then models that also see images, then live omni streaming with voice, and finally full-duplex. The rising band labelled human-like interaction is the direction of travel. MiniCPM-o 4.5 places itself alone in the last box. Treat it as the authors' framing of the field rather than as a result.

label: Fig. 3
text: Perception and speech overlap only in the full-duplex panel on the right. In traditional streaming the model perceives, then speaks, so while it says the player in red is dribbling, it misses the shot. In full-duplex it keeps watching while talking and can break in with he shoots. The two red flaws at the bottom, blocked input and passive behaviour, are the problems the rest of the paper solves.

label: Fig. 4
text: Time runs left to right in one-second columns, and the rows go from raw streams at the bottom to audio output at the top. Each second, three visual and two audio embedding groups enter the language model. In the first second it only emits a silent token. Later chunks start with a speak token and a few words, and each word with its hidden state h feeds the speech decoders. This is the full architecture running live.

label: Fig. 5
text: Filled gold dots are speech tokens and light dots are text tokens. In row a, all the text is written first, so it runs far ahead of the voice. In row b, a fixed ratio assumes every word takes the same time to say. Row c is TAIL: each second carries however many words fit into about one second of speech, four, two, three, then one here. Counts are schematic.

label: Fig. 6
text: Accuracy reward rises over 400 reinforcement learning steps for three runs; the curves are redrawn by shape, so read trends rather than exact values. All three climb from about 0.76 to about 0.79. The Kimi-style length reward peaks near step 250 and then drops, while the paper's smoother reward from equation one tracks the baseline without any length reward. It supports the choice of equation one.

Each row changes one Omni-Flow design choice: chunk size, whether chunk boundaries are marked, and whether the model first decides listen or speak before choosing words. The winning row, in green, is one-second chunks, explicit boundaries and the listen-speak control. Very short chunks of 0.2 or 0.1 seconds hurt almost every score, because each chunk holds too little information to decide well.

Indigo bars are MMLU, a text knowledge test, and gold bars are SDQA, spoken question answering, for the five settings in Table 1. The left pair is highest on both. Shrinking chunks to 0.2 or 0.1 seconds cuts spoken question answering from 0.36 to about 0.1. The lesson is a latency against capacity trade-off: faster refresh leaves less room to think in each chunk.

Rows are vision benchmarks in five groups and columns are models, with MiniCPM-o in the last column and the best score in each row in green. Lower is better only where marked with a down arrow. MiniCPM-o wins many rows, and it is clearly best on OmniDocBench document parsing, while Gemini 2.5 Flash leads on MMMU and long video. This backs the claim of near-Gemini vision at nine billion parameters.

Thinking mode means the model reasons step by step before answering, and this table repeats the vision comparison in that mode, now including GPT-5. MiniCPM-o is best on MMBench English and on OCRBench, while GPT-5 leads on MMMU, MathVista and instruction following. The gap to proprietary models is small on documents and larger on expert reasoning.

Speech understanding is tested on recognition, translation, audio understanding and spoken question answering. For speech recognition lower error is better. MiniCPM-o is close to the best at recognition and wins GigaSpeech and VoxPopuli, and it leads clearly on Speech TriviaQA with 75.5. It trails on Speech Web Questions and Chinese knowledge questions. For your own project, this means spoken questions are understood well without a separate speech-to-text model.

Speech generation is judged by error rate when the output is transcribed, lower is better, and by speaker similarity. MiniCPM-o has the lowest error on both Seed TTS sets, and on long English speech its word error rate is 3.37 against about 15 and 17 for the others. It also leads on emotion and style control. CosyVoice2 keeps a slight edge in voice similarity.

This table checks whether adding images and speech damaged the language model. MiniCPM-o is compared with its own backbone, Qwen3 eight B Instruct, on text-only tests. The average rises slightly, from 81.6 to 82.1, with a big gain on BBH reasoning, but MMLU drops about five points and Math 500 about seven. So text skill is mostly kept, a useful point when you fine-tune only the language model part.

These benchmarks give the model video and audio together, in normal turn-based mode. MiniCPM-o wins five of seven, including a large lead on Video-Holmes with 64.3, while Qwen3-Omni wins FutureOmni and Gemini wins Video-MME-Short with audio. The result supports the claim that a nine billion parameter model can beat a thirty billion mixture-of-experts omni model on joint audio and video understanding.

This is the only full-duplex result, and it is vision only, because audio full-duplex benchmarks barely exist. On live sports commentary, MiniCPM-o reaches a win rate of 54.4 against 41.5 and 45.6 for two streaming video models. Treat it as encouraging evidence for Omni-Flow, but note that the paper does not measure full-duplex speech quantitatively.

This ablation compares three length rewards in reinforcement learning, showing benchmark average and how much shorter the answers became. The Kimi-style reward cuts thinking length by about half but lowers accuracy, while the paper's reward cuts it by about a third and raises the thinking average to 74.3. Figure 6 shows why: the aggressive reward stalls training.

Three speech generation modes are compared on the same test set. Fixed-ratio interleaving gives the lowest error rates. TAIL, the time-aligned mode used for full-duplex, raises English word error rate from 2.38 to 3.93 while keeping similar voice quality. That is the honest cost of staying on the clock: a little accuracy is traded for speech that matches the live scene.

Efficiency is measured on one RTX 4090 graphics card. In sixteen-bit precision Qwen3-Omni does not fit at all, while MiniCPM-o needs 19 gigabytes. With four-bit weights MiniCPM-o needs 11 gigabytes and gives 212 tokens per second, about half the memory of Qwen3-Omni. These numbers tell you what to expect on a free Colab GPU with 16 gigabytes.

Real-time factor is processing time divided by audio length, so anything below one keeps up with live speech. Plain PyTorch in four bits reaches 1.26, too slow for real time, while the authors' llama.cpp-omni reaches about 0.2 with 11 gigabytes. The engine matters as much as the precision for live streaming.

Bars show inference memory for each framework and precision, and the rust dashed line marks the 16 gigabytes of a free Colab T4. Only the four-bit settings fall below it. Remember these are inference numbers; QLoRA training adds activations and adapter optimizer state, so you must check on your own GPU before planning the experiment.

The appendix lists the size of every component. The language model dominates with about 8.2 billion of the 9.34 billion parameters; SigLIP has about 0.42 billion, Whisper about 0.31 billion, and the projectors are tiny at 21 and 11 million. When you choose where to put LoRA adapters, this table tells you which linear layers exist and how wide they are, for example hidden size 4096 in the backbone.

Use this box to plan your fine-tuning and experiments. All three inputs are native, so you can skip a speech-to-text pipeline. The main risk is memory: load the model in four bits, freeze the encoders, put LoRA on the backbone's attention and MLP layers, and test on a T4 early. A spoken question about a document photo plays to its strengths, and an English versus Arabic comparison gives a clear fairness experiment.

label: Primer
text: Every input has to become a row of vectors before the language model can read it. An image slice passes through the SigLIP vision transformer, which gives 1024 vectors, and a resampler squeezes them to 64. Sound is drawn as a log-mel spectrogram, the Whisper encoder makes 50 frames a second, and a small MLP merges every five into one, giving ten tokens a second. This is exactly what you should be able to explain first.

label: Primer
text: The top timeline is the usual turn-based model: while it answers, new input is ignored. The bottom timeline is full-duplex, the paper's main idea. Time is cut into one-second chunks, and each chunk holds three groups of visual tokens, two groups of audio tokens, and then the model's output. When there is nothing to say, the output is a single listen token, so the model decides by itself when to talk.

label: Primer
text: Speech can be written as tokens too, about twenty five per second. Asking the big language model to write all of them would slow it and hurt its language skill, so MiniCPM-o keeps it on text, three to four steps a second. A small speech decoder takes each text token plus the model's hidden state and writes the S3 speech tokens, and a flow-matching decoder turns them into sound in a reference voice.

label: Primer
text: MiniCPM-o 4.5 comes after Qwen3-Omni, the larger reference model, and before Gemma 4. Qwen3-Omni uses a thirty billion parameter mixture of experts, while this is a single nine billion parameter dense model that adds full-duplex interaction. Gemma 4 answers only in text. The coloured chips show that text, images and voice are all native inputs, and the rust bar is the part you would fine-tune with LoRA.

Keep this list open while you read. The most important terms are full-duplex, meaning the model listens while it talks, Omni-Flow with its listen token, and the chain from Whisper and SigLIP into the Qwen3 eight B backbone. For your experiments, note word error rate, which you may use as a metric, and the memory figures: for inference, sixteen bit weights need nineteen gigabytes, while four bit weights fit in eleven.

Gemma 4 asks how far a family of open models can go in reading text, images and audio while staying small enough for phones and free GPUs. The answer is a set of decoder-only models, from E2B with 2.3 billion effective parameters up to a 31 billion dense model and a 26 billion Mixture-of-Experts, that take all three inputs and reply in text. The small models attach frozen image and audio encoders, and the 12B model drops the encoders entirely. The tab opens with the input paths, then the problems, the method with Algorithm 1, the display math, the two figures, all twelve tables, and a box on putting it into practice. Gemma 4 is the last of the eleven papers, after MiniCPM-o 4.5, and closes the omni group that started with MiniMind-O.

label: Overview
text: Read this diagram row by row: indigo is text, teal is images, gold is audio, and each row runs from raw input to tokens inside the one decoder. Notice what is missing: video has no path and nothing produces speech. The bottom band shows the paper's highlight, the 12B model, where one linear layer replaces each encoder. Everything else in the tab explains one of these boxes.

label: Problem A
text: This stacked bar shows where the E2B model's roughly 5.1 billion stored parameters go, drawn to scale from Table 1. Per-layer embedding tables are the biggest slice, which is why the model is called 2.3 billion effective. The audio and vision encoders together add almost half a billion parameters. That overhead motivates both the smaller audio encoder and the encoder-free 12B design.

label: Problem B
text: Each model gets two bars: indigo for bf16 weights and rust for the quantized release, in gigabytes, from Table 3. Quantization shrinks E2B from 4.6 to 0.8 gigabytes and the 31B from 64 to about 19. The KV cache for 32 thousand tokens stays small, from 0.05 to 1.1 gigabytes, thanks to the attention design explained in Method 1.

These six steps follow one prompt through the model. First the conversation is wrapped in turn tokens. Then text is tokenized, images are resized and pooled into soft tokens, and audio is encoded in 40 millisecond chunks. All of these vectors enter the same decoder, which mixes local and global attention. Finally the model may write a thinking trace before its answer, while the drafter speeds up decoding. It is the skeleton of a one-page explanation of the inputs.

label: Method 1
text: Five indigo boxes are local layers that only look at a sliding window of recent tokens; the magenta box is a global layer that sees the whole context. Only global layers need a long KV cache, and there the model reuses keys as values and uses p-RoPE, cutting that cache by 37.5 percent. The small models instead share KV caches across layers. This is the fix for the memory problem in Problem B.

label: Method 2
text: Two ways to turn audio into LLM input. In E2B and E4B, Mel features pass through two downsampling convolutions and twelve frozen Conformer layers. In 12B, each raw 40 millisecond chunk of 640 samples goes through a single linear projection, and images get the same treatment with one 35 million parameter matmul. Table 8 later shows the encoder-free 12B still transcribes well.

label: Method 3
text: Quantization-aware training means the model learns with quantized weights in the loop, so the low-bit files keep their quality. Gemma 4 ships a mobile format with int2 and int4 weights and int8 activations, and a blockwise four-bit format called Q four underscore zero. The encoders are quantized too: the audio encoder falls from 390 to 87 megabytes. Per-block scales also keep fp16 inference stable, which matters on a T4.

Algorithm 1 picks an image size that respects the token budget while keeping the shape. It computes the side of one pooled patch, the pixel area the budget allows, and a single scale factor for both sides. Then it rounds each side down to whole pooled patches, so the budget is never exceeded, and resizes bicubically. Figure 2 runs this procedure on a real example.

label: Alg. 1
text: The first three lines of Algorithm 1. m equals k times p: the side of a pooled patch, k by k patches of p pixels each. T equals N max times m squared: the pixel area the token budget allows. f is the square root of T over H times W: one scale factor applied to both height and width so the area lands near T.

label: Alg. 1
text: Rounding down is what keeps the image within budget. H target is f times H divided by m, rounded down to a whole number, times m, and the same for the width. Because both sides shrink to whole pooled patches, the number of soft tokens can only be at or below N max. The aspect ratio is kept mostly, not exactly.

The soft-token count is the number of pooled patches along the height times the number along the width, and it never exceeds N max. The ViT itself sees k squared times as many patches, nine times more with a three by three pool. This line is implied by Figure 2 rather than printed in the paper.

label: Fig. 2
text: A worked example with the Figure 2 numbers. With a pool of three and patches of 16 pixels, m is 48, and a budget of ten tokens allows 23,040 pixels. The scale factor is about 0.198, which gives 96 by 192 pixels after rounding down, so eight soft tokens from 72 patches. You can reuse this calculation to predict your own image token counts.

Sixteen thousand samples per second times 40 milliseconds gives 640 samples per chunk. In the encoder-free 12B, each such chunk is a 640-dimensional vector projected straight into the LLM, with no extra position code because audio is already ordered in time. For your pipeline, make sure audio is resampled to 16 kilohertz.

A 48 by 48 RGB patch holds 6,912 numbers. In the 12B model a single matrix of about 35 million parameters maps each patch into the LLM embedding space, a 2D coordinate position embedding is added, and a LayerNorm follows. This replaces the 550 million parameter ViT used by the larger models.

The drafter's final projection normally scores all 262 thousand vocabulary entries. For E2B and E4B it is replaced by a top-k selection over clusters of tokens, so the matrix shrinks from d by 262,000 to d by 4,096, where d is the drafter's width. The paper reports a similar acceptance rate, so drafting gets cheaper without losing accepted tokens.

label: Fig. 1
text: Grey blocks are the main model, magenta blocks are the multi-token prediction drafter. Each drafter step joins the newest token's embedding with the previous hidden state, runs four small layers that cross-attend to the main model's KV cache, and predicts one more token. The main model then checks the drafted tokens in one pass. This speeds up decoding but does not change what the model understands.

label: Fig. 2
text: On the left is the original 572 by 1024 image; on the right, the resized 96 by 192 version cut into eight 48 pixel pooled patches, each made of nine 16 pixel patches. The ViT encodes 72 patches, pooling merges each group of nine, and the LLM receives eight soft tokens. This is Algorithm 1 in action, with a tiny budget chosen for illustration.

label: Chart 1
text: Dark teal bars use 1120 image tokens, light bars use 280, for each model size. Every model loses accuracy on InfographicVQA with fewer tokens, and the encoder-free 12B loses most, falling from 88.4 to 58.7. E2B drops from 63.9 to 44.6. For document images in your task, the token budget is a memory versus accuracy trade-off.

label: Chart 2
text: Word error rate per language, lower is better, for Gemma 4 E2B in gold, Gemma 4 E4B in indigo and Gemma 3n E4B in grey. Gemma 4 improves the average from 0.085 to 0.075. Arabic is the exception: E4B scores 0.162 against 0.101 for the older model. That gap is a ready-made fairness question for your own project.

Parameter counts for each model, split into audio encoder, vision encoder, embedder, the transformer weights called einsums, and the drafter. Only E2B and E4B list an audio encoder, and the 12B lists no encoders at all. The large second embedder number in E2B and E4B is per-layer embeddings. Check this table before choosing which model can take voice input.

Hardware used for pre-training: thousands of TPU chips per model, with the work split across data, sequence and replica shards. The 12B used the most chips, on older v4 TPUs. It is context only; you will not reproduce pre-training, but it shows why you fine-tune rather than train from scratch.

Memory for text-only weights in bf16 and in the quantized release, plus the extra int8 KV cache for 32 thousand tokens. E2B needs 4.6 gigabytes in bf16 and 0.8 in the mobile format. These numbers are your starting point for deciding whether a model fits a 16 gigabyte T4, before adding image and audio activations.

Arena Text ranks models by blind human votes, turned into Elo scores. Gemma 4 31B, at rank 43, is the best dense open model, and the 26B Mixture-of-Experts sits near models with hundreds of billions of parameters. Gemma 3 27B, far below at rank 157, shows the generational jump.

Text benchmarks for all Gemma 4 sizes in thinking mode against Gemma 3 27B without thinking. The 31B wins almost every row. Note the small models: E2B roughly matches Gemma 3 27B on several tasks with about ten times fewer parameters, although on hard reasoning such as AIME the gap to larger Gemma 4 models is large.

Vision benchmarks at the maximum budget of 1120 image tokens. OmniDocBench is an error score, so lower is better there. E4B matches or beats Gemma 3 27B on these tasks, and even E2B reaches 63.9 on InfographicVQA. Compare with Table 12 to see the cost of fewer tokens.

The same vision benchmarks at a budget of 280 image tokens. Scores fall for every model, most sharply on the document tasks InfographicVQA and OmniDocBench, and most of all for the encoder-free 12B. If you lower the budget to save GPU memory, expect this kind of drop on document images.

Speech translation into English on CoVoST, scored with BLEU, higher is better, where the model first transcribes and then translates. Gemma 4 E4B is best in every column, averaging 38.2, and both Gemma 4 models beat Gemma 3n while using an audio encoder under a quarter of the size on disk.

Speech recognition on FLEURS, as word error rate or character error rate, lower is better. Gemma 4 E4B is best in eleven of twelve languages and on average. Arabic is the exception, where Gemma 3n E4B stays better. When you compute WER in your own experiments, normalization choices will change these numbers.

Audio results for the encoder-free 12B, which has no audio encoder at all. Its transcription errors are close to or below those of E4B, for example 0.070 in Arabic, and its translation BLEU is similar. The claim this supports is that raw audio chunks and a linear projection can be enough.

Long-context tests: RULER accuracy, retrieval recall, graph reasoning and translating a new language from a grammar book. Gemma 4 models beat Gemma 3 27B widely, E4B included. E2B weakens at 128 thousand tokens. Typical fine-tuning inputs are short, so this matters mostly as evidence that the attention design works.

The two Vision Transformer sizes: the 550 million parameter encoder has width 1152 and 27 layers, and the 150 million one used by E2B and E4B has width 768 and 16 layers. Both use 16 pixel patches. The smaller encoder is the one you will meet on a free GPU.

The chat format of the instruction-tuned models. Each turn starts with a turn token and a role, and ends with the end-of-turn token. A think token in the system turn switches on the reasoning trace, and tools use their own tags. For fine-tuning, format every training example this way and end targets with the end-of-turn token.

Use E2B or E4B so voice, image and text are all native, and add an ASR model only if you pick 26B or 31B. Load in four bits, put LoRA on the decoder's attention and MLP layers, keep the encoders frozen, and format data with the chat template. A spoken question about a document image matches what the paper tests, and Arabic versus English speech gives a clear fairness split.

label: Primer
text: An image enters Gemma 4 as a few soft tokens, not as pixels. The picture is resized to fit a token budget, cut into sixteen pixel patches, encoded by a frozen Vision Transformer, and each three by three group is pooled into one token. You pick the budget, from 70 to 1120 tokens; fewer tokens save memory but hurt document images. The magenta shortcut is the 12B model, which replaces the whole encoder with one linear layer.

label: Primer
text: Speech reaches the language model as a stream of vectors, never as text. Sound at sixteen kilohertz is cut into forty millisecond chunks of 640 samples. In E2B and E4B each chunk becomes a Mel filterbank and passes a frozen Conformer encoder of 305 million parameters; the 12B model projects the raw samples with one linear layer. Either way the model answers in text, so for your pipeline, resample audio to sixteen kilohertz.

label: Primer
text: This chart answers the first practical question: which model fits your free GPU? Outlined bars are weights in bf16, solid bars the paper's quantized files, and the magenta line is the sixteen gigabyte T4. E2B and E4B are called effective sizes because per-layer embeddings sit on top, and the 26B Mixture-of-Experts uses only about four billion parameters per token but must still be fully loaded. Encoders, activations and LoRA add more, so start with E2B or E4B.

label: Primer
text: Gemma 4 is the eleventh and final paper of the atlas. Before it, MiniCPM-o 4.5 showed one nine billion parameter model that sees, hears and talks back. Gemma 4 instead offers five sizes with small frozen encoders, and a 12B model with no encoders at all. It reads text, images and, on three sizes, speech, but it only writes text. After this tab, the next step is your own fine-tuned model.

These fourteen terms are the vocabulary the paper assumes. Model names carry meaning: E2B means about two billion effective parameters, and A4B means about four billion active parameters in a Mixture-of-Experts. Soft tokens, Mel filterbanks and Conformers describe how images and sound get in. WER, CER, BLEU, FLEURS and CoVoST are how the paper scores speech, and you will reuse WER in your own evaluation. Come back here whenever a table uses a name you do not know.
